# Product: a complete backend platform

Source: https://cubibase.com/product

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/product.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

How CubiBase fits together: a dedicated PostgreSQL database per project, Authentication, Storage, and Functions on one project host, managed from one Console.

## Architecture

- Control plane (`api.cubibase.com`): developer accounts, projects, schema management, keys, logs, billing. Authenticated with a session JWT or personal access token (`cb_pat_`).
- Data plane (`{slug}.api.cubibase.com`): REST rows, RPC, end-user auth, storage, function invocation. Identified by a publishable key (`cb_pub_`), authorized by an end-user JWT or a project secret key (`cb_sec_`, service actor).
- Every project database has four NOSUPERUSER, NOBYPASSRLS roles: DDL, API, SQL, auth.
- Row-level security is always enforced; `cubibase.current_user_id()` and `cubibase.current_role()` are available inside policies.

## Docs

- Introduction: https://cubibase.com/docs
- Architecture detail: https://cubibase.com/docs/architecture
- API routes: https://cubibase.com/docs/reference/routes
- Error codes: https://cubibase.com/docs/reference/errors

# CubiBase pricing

Source: https://cubibase.com/pricing

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/pricing.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Three plans. Every plan includes one project. Add more projects for $9/month each on Pro and Business. Every plan includes a PostgreSQL database per project, authentication, REST API, storage, and Functions. Prices in USD; paid plans bill monthly through Stripe, self-serve in the Console. Database storage is allocated per project; all other consumption quotas are shared across your organization. Upgrade your plan without changing your project count.

## Plans

| Plan | Price | Projects | Database size | File storage | Total bandwidth | Monthly active users | API requests | Function invocations | Function compute |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 forever | 1 | 500 MB per project | 2 GB shared | 15 GB per month · shared | 50,000 shared | 500,000 per month · shared | 500,000 per month · shared | 10,000 GB-seconds per month · shared |
| Pro | $25/month | 1 included · $9/mo each additional | 10 GB per project | 100 GB shared | 500 GB per month · shared | 100,000 shared | 1,000,000 per month · shared | 2,000,000 per month · shared | 50,000 GB-seconds per month · shared |
| Business | $99/month | 1 included · $9/mo each additional | 10 GB per project | 250 GB shared | 750 GB per month · shared | 500,000 shared | 5,000,000 per month · shared | 6,000,000 per month · shared | 300,000 GB-seconds per month · shared |

### Free — $0

For side projects and first prototypes.

- A PostgreSQL database per project
- Auth: email + password, TOTP MFA
- REST API for exposed tables
- Storage: public and private buckets
- Functions: TypeScript/JavaScript on 4 trigger types
- Console: tables, rows, SQL, keys, files, functions
- MCP, CLI and Agent Skills included
- Upgrade to Pro for additional projects
- Paused after 14 days without activity

### Pro — $25/month

For products with real users.

- Everything in Free
- Additional projects at $9/month, each with its own database
- Daily backups kept 7 days
- Never paused for inactivity
- Bring your own IdP (RS256 / JWKS)
- Priority email support

### Business — $99/month

For teams running several client apps.

- Everything in Pro
- 1 included project · additional at $9/month
- Daily backups kept 14 days
- Highest shared quotas: MAU, bandwidth, functions
- Onboarding help and a named support contact

## Included on every plan

- **A PostgreSQL database per project** — Each project gets its own database, with tables, rows, and SQL in the Console.
- **REST API** — Expose a table and call it over HTTPS with your project keys.
- **Authentication** — Email and password sign-in, sessions, and TOTP multi-factor authentication.
- **Row-level security** — Policies and user columns limit each request to the rows it may read.
- **File storage** — Public and private buckets, with signed links for private files.
- **Functions** — TypeScript or JavaScript on HTTP, database, storage, and cron triggers.

| MCP, CLI and Agent Skills | yes | yes | yes |
| Support | Email | Priority email | Priority + onboarding |

## Additional usage (Pro & Business)

Need more resources? Enable additional usage on your paid plan and pay only for what you consume. Set a monthly spending limit to remain in control of your costs.

| Resource | Price | Billing unit | How it is measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL storage | $0.20 per GB-month | GB-month | Time-weighted excess capacity across the billing period — you pay for how much and how long, not the peak |
| File storage | $0.03 per GB-month | GB-month | Time-weighted excess capacity across the billing period — you pay for how much and how long, not the peak |
| File bandwidth (preview rate) | $0.03 per GB | GB | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |
| API bandwidth (preview rate) | $0.09 per GB | GB | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |
| API requests (preview rate) | $3 per million requests | 1 million requests | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |
| CDN requests (preview rate) | $4 per million requests | 1 million requests | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |
| Authentication (preview rate) | $0.50 per 1,000 additional MAU | 1,000 additional MAU | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |
| Function invocations (preview rate) | $1 per million invocations | 1 million invocations | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |
| Function compute (preview rate) | $3 per 100,000 GB-seconds | 100,000 GB-seconds | Cumulative usage above the included monthly quota |

Preview pricing: the database and file storage rates are final. The other rates are the current implementation rates, validated against infrastructure costs before general availability. You always review and accept the exact rates shown in the Console before any additional-usage charge can accrue.

- **Off until you turn it on** — Additional usage is disabled by default. Nothing is metered for payment until an organization owner or billing admin enables it in Console → Billing → Additional Usage and accepts the pricing. Without activation, quotas keep refusing operations exactly as before — there are no automatic unexpected charges.
- **Paid plans only** — Free does not support paid overages. Additional usage is available on Pro and Business, at the same rates on both plans.
- **Spending limits you control** — Choose a monthly limit for additional usage — $5, $10, $25, $50, $100, a custom amount, or no limit with explicit confirmation. Limits cover additional resource usage only, never your base plan, additional projects, prorations or taxes. Alerts arrive at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100% of the limit; at the limit, new billable consumption is blocked where technically possible while included quotas, billing access and deletion keep working. Metering delays (especially CDN traffic and ongoing storage) mean a small bounded overshoot is possible — the limit is a control, not an absolute invoice cap.
- **Storage bills by time, not by peak** — Database and file storage overages use time-weighted excess capacity (GB-month): holding 50 GB over your allowance for half a month bills about half of a full month. Database excess is measured independently per project — spare capacity in one database never offsets another database’s excess.
- **No double billing on bandwidth** — API bandwidth is part of your total bandwidth allowance. API traffic beyond the API sublimit bills at the API rate; file delivery uses whatever included total bandwidth remains. The same outbound byte is never billed twice and there is no separate total-bandwidth charge.
- **API and CDN requests are independent** — API request and CDN request quotas are counted separately: one API request served through the CDN consumes both. If both allowances are exhausted and additional usage is enabled, both overage rates apply to that request.
- **Projects stay a flat add-on** — Additional projects remain $9/month each — a fixed subscription item, not metered usage. Shared organization quotas do not grow with additional projects; only the per-project database comes with each one.
- **Billing units for overages** — Included quotas use binary units (1 GB = 1024 MB), unchanged. Overage billing uses decimal units (1 GB = 1,000 MB = 1,000,000,000 bytes); only the excess above your included quota is converted and billed. Usage is aggregated continuously and reported to Stripe hourly; the Usage page always shows the live estimate, and the Stripe invoice is the final word.

Enable additional usage and set your spending limit in Console → Billing → Additional Usage (https://console.cubibase.com/billing/additional-usage).

## Pricing FAQ

**How do I pay for Pro or Business?**

In the Console. Choose Get Pro or Get Business, sign in, and complete the Stripe checkout on the Billing page. Payment methods, invoices, plan changes, and cancellation are managed there too. Prices on this page are the published monthly rates.

**Are quotas per project or per organization?**

Database storage is allocated per project. All other consumption quotas are shared across your organization. Each project has its own PostgreSQL database with an independent storage quota (500 MB on Free, 10 GB on paid plans and additional projects). Monthly active users, API requests, bandwidth, object storage, storage operations, download requests, CloudFront requests, and Function invocations and compute are pooled across all projects in your organization. Buying additional projects adds project slots and per-project database storage — it never increases the shared quotas.

**How do additional projects work?**

Every plan includes one project. On Pro and Business, each additional project is $9/month with its own 10 GB database; Free cannot purchase additional projects — upgrade to Pro first. Project billing follows your actual project count: when you create a project, Stripe adds $9/month prorated for the rest of your cycle (the Console shows the exact next-invoice preview before you confirm); when you delete one, the quantity drops and Stripe credits the unused time on the next invoice. Your billing cycle does not reset. Switching between Pro and Business keeps your project count and charges unchanged. Additional projects are a fixed subscription item — they are never part of metered additional usage. Example: Pro with 5 projects is $61/month ($25 + 4 × $9).

**What counts as a monthly active user?**

An end user who authenticates at least once during the billing cycle, counted once per organization across all projects. Users from your own identity provider are not counted. MAU is a shared organization quota, not a per-project registered-user count.

**What happens when I reach a quota?**

By default, the affected operation is refused with a clear error showing the limit and your reset date, and the Console warns you at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100% utilization. Nothing is billed automatically. If the account stays over its plan limits for 7 days, its projects are suspended until you upgrade or reduce usage. On Pro and Business you can instead enable additional usage (Console → Billing → Additional Usage): consumption beyond the included quota then bills at the published per-unit rates under a monthly spending limit you choose. Nothing is ever deleted because a quota was reached, and projects reactivate automatically once the account fits its plan. Upgrading raises the limits on the same projects and databases.

**How do the file storage quotas work?**

Object storage is one shared organization capacity (2 GB on Free, 100 GB on Pro, 250 GB on Business), enforced on the server before an upload is authorized, so concurrent uploads cannot exceed it. File delivery draws on your shared total bandwidth allowance (see the bandwidth FAQ below). Maximum single file size is 50 MB, 1 GB, or 5 GB by plan. Reaching a storage limit blocks new uploads or downloads but never deletes files; deleting objects frees capacity immediately. Sizes use binary units (1 GB = 1024 MB).

**How does bandwidth accounting work?**

Total bandwidth is one shared organization allowance covering everything delivered to your users: API responses and file downloads (15 GB on Free, 500 GB on Pro, 750 GB on Business per month). API bandwidth is a sublimit of that total, not an extra allowance (5 GB, 25 GB, 100 GB): on Pro, using the full 25 GB of API bandwidth still leaves 475 GB for file delivery. Hitting the API sublimit never blocks your remaining file bandwidth. Bandwidth counts outbound bytes delivered to customers — not uploads or internal transfers — and resets with your billing cycle. Sizes use binary units (1 GB = 1024 MB).

**How do CubiBase Functions quotas work?**

Functions are included on every plan: TypeScript/JavaScript code triggered by HTTP, database events, storage events, or cron schedules. Function count, concurrency and schedules are limited per project; invocations and compute (GB-seconds) are metered per organization per billing cycle, shared across all projects. Every executed run counts — success, failure and timeout alike — while requests rejected by the gateway (auth, signature, quota) are not counted. At a limit, new invocations are refused until the cycle resets or you upgrade — unless you have enabled additional usage on a paid plan, in which case excess invocations and compute bill at the published rates under your spending limit. The Console's Usage page always shows the live values.

**What is additional usage, and how do I enable it?**

Additional usage lets Pro and Business organizations keep consuming resources beyond the included quotas and pay only for the excess, at the per-unit rates in the Additional Usage table above. It is disabled by default: an organization owner or billing admin enables it in Console → Billing → Additional Usage, reviews the exact rates, and chooses a monthly spending limit ($5, $10, $25, $50, $100, a custom amount, or no limit with explicit confirmation). Until then, quotas behave exactly as before — operations are refused at the limit and nothing is billed automatically. Free does not support paid overages. Disabling additional usage stops future metered charges but does not cancel usage already validly accrued.

**Is the spending limit a guaranteed cap on my invoice?**

It is a spending control, not an absolute guarantee. CubiBase meters usage continuously and blocks new billable consumption when the estimated additional-usage spend reaches your limit, but some metering sources — especially CDN traffic and ongoing storage capacity — arrive with a delay, so a small bounded overshoot is possible. The limit applies to additional resource usage only; your base plan, additional projects, prorations and taxes are separate. Alerts arrive at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100% of the limit, and billing access, included quotas and deletion always keep working.

**How are storage overages calculated?**

By time-weighted excess capacity, not peak size. Database storage is measured independently per project: only the part above your per-project allowance bills, and unused capacity in one database never offsets another database’s excess. File storage is one shared organization capacity. In both cases the excess is integrated over time as GB-months: holding 50 GB over the allowance for half a billing period costs about half of the full-month rate. Included quotas use binary units (1 GB = 1024 MB); overage billing uses decimal GB (1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes) applied only to the excess.

**Can one request be charged twice — API and CDN?**

API request and CDN request quotas are independent: an API request served through the CDN consumes both allowances, and if both are exhausted with additional usage enabled, both overage rates apply (at the current rates, one million such requests would bill $3 for API requests plus $4 for CDN requests). Bandwidth is different: each outbound byte is billed at most once — API traffic beyond the API sublimit bills at the API bandwidth rate, file delivery uses the remaining included total bandwidth, and there is no separate total-bandwidth charge.

**Are the additional usage rates final?**

Preview pricing: the database and file storage rates are final. The other rates are the current implementation rates, validated against infrastructure costs before general availability. You always review and accept the exact rates shown in the Console before any additional-usage charge can accrue.

**What happens to a Free project I stop using?**

After 14 days without activity (no API, auth, or Console use) a Free project is paused and we email you. Resume it from the Console within 60 days and it is back instantly — the database is untouched. After 60 days paused we take a full PostgreSQL backup (.backup file), keep it, and remove the live database to stop storage costs. You can download the backup anytime, and resuming an archived project restores the database automatically. Pro and Business projects are never paused for inactivity.

**Is there an uptime SLA?**

No plan publishes an uptime percentage or a service-level agreement today. Support tiers describe how your email is queued, not a response-time guarantee.

**Are backups included?**

Paid plans include daily database backups: kept 7 days on Pro and 14 days on Business. Archived Free projects get a full PostgreSQL backup (.backup, pg_dump custom format) that is kept and downloadable from the Console, and resuming restores it automatically. Free does not include a daily backup schedule for active projects — plan your own export routine for data you cannot lose.

Quota model (catalog v4.5): database storage per project; all other consumption quotas shared per organization. Additional projects increase project slots only — shared quotas stay unchanged. No uptime SLA is published. This page describes the product, not a service-level agreement.

title: A real PostgreSQL database for every project.
text:
# A real PostgreSQL database for every project.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/postgresql

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/postgresql.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Every CubiBase project gets its own PostgreSQL database. It is ready when provisioning finishes, other projects cannot query it, and your tables are ordinary PostgreSQL tables you design in the Console and expose over REST.

## At a glance

- **One database per project** — One slug maps to one database. Requests to the project host reach only that database; other projects cannot query it.
- **Provisioning as a job** — The Console shows provisioning, active, or failed. A failed provision can be retried by the project owner.
- **Ordinary PostgreSQL tables** — uuid, text, integer, bigint, boolean, timestamptz, jsonb, numeric, and double precision, with one primary key per table.
- **Four roles, no superuser** — DDL, API, SQL, and auth roles. Each is NOSUPERUSER and NOBYPASSRLS.
- **Managed schemas** — Your tables in public; auth, logs, vault, and storage managed by CubiBase alongside them.
- **Read-only SQL editor** — One statement on the SQL role inside a read-only transaction. Schema changes go through the Database screens.

## What “dedicated” means here

Each project has a slug, a status, and its own database. Your application data goes in that database. Your developer account, Console sessions, and the list of your projects are stored separately.

- One slug, such as example-project, maps to one database, such as example_project_db.
- Requests are routed by the project host, such as example-project.api.cubibase.com. A client cannot point a request at another project.
- Provisioning is a job. The Console can show whether the project is still provisioning, active, or failed.
- A failed provision can be retried by the project owner. A retry does not create a second database for a project that is already active.

## You still use SQL

Tables you create through CubiBase are ordinary PostgreSQL tables in the public schema. Column types include uuid, text, integer, bigint, boolean, timestamptz, jsonb, numeric, and double precision. A table needs exactly one primary key.

The Console SQL editor is for reading. It runs one read-only statement on a SQL role inside a read-only transaction. Changing columns is a schema operation, not an ad hoc script in that box.

## Four roles, none of them a superuser

Provisioning creates four login roles for the project database. Each is NOSUPERUSER and NOBYPASSRLS.

- The DDL role owns the tables you create from the Console.
- The API role runs Data API requests, and only after you grant an operation by exposing it.
- The SQL role serves the Console row browser and the read-only SQL editor.
- The auth role runs the sign-up, sign-in, and session flows against the managed auth schema.

## Schemas the platform manages

Your tables live in public. Alongside it, provisioning creates managed schemas: auth holds end users, refresh sessions, and MFA factors; logs holds request and auth events written by CubiBase; vault holds project secrets that no request role can read; storage holds the bucket and object catalog for file storage.

The SQL role can read auth tables and logs from the Console SQL editor. The Data API serves public tables you expose, and the auth endpoints are the application path to user accounts.

## FAQ

**When does the database exist?**

After the provisioning job completes and the project status is active. Registration of the project alone does not create the database.

**Can two apps share one CubiBase database?**

Put them in the same project only if they should share that database. If they should be isolated, create two projects. CubiBase does not offer a shared schema as a substitute for a separate database.

## Related

- [Authentication](https://cubibase.com/features/authentication) — The auth schema and the sign-up endpoints in that database.
- [Database management](https://cubibase.com/features/database-management) — Create tables and inspect rows from the Console.
- [REST API](https://cubibase.com/features/rest-api) — Call the database from your application.
- [Quickstart](https://cubibase.com/docs/quickstart) — The path from an empty project to a first request.

# Sign-up and sign-in for your application users.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/authentication

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/authentication.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Every project includes CubiBase Auth: email and password, anonymous sign-ins that convert into real accounts, Google sign-in, and TOTP multi-factor. Users live in your project database, and the access token they receive is the JWT your Data API calls already use.

## At a glance

- **Email + password** — Signup and sign-in at /auth/v1. Passwords are stored only as Argon2id hashes in your own database.
- **Anonymous sign-ins** — Visitors get a real session without credentials, then convert in place — same user id, sessions, and data.
- **Google sign-in** — Built-in OAuth/OIDC with a browser redirect flow or a verified Google ID token from your mobile or web app.
- **TOTP multi-factor** — Enroll an authenticator app per user; make MFA optional or required for the whole project.
- **Rotating sessions** — Access tokens live one hour, refresh tokens 30 days. Reuse of a retired token revokes the whole family.
- **Bring your own IdP** — Configure a JWKS URL, issuer, and audience and CubiBase verifies RS256 tokens on every Data API request.

## The flows your app calls

All auth endpoints live on the project host under /auth/v1 and require the apikey header, the same publishable key as the Data API. The user’s password travels in the request body over HTTPS and is never stored in plain text.

- POST /auth/v1/signup creates a user and returns a session: user, accessToken, refreshToken, expiresIn.
- POST /auth/v1/signup/anonymous creates a session without credentials, when the project allows it.
- POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=password signs a user in with email and password.
- POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token exchanges a refresh token for a new session.
- POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=id_token verifies a Google ID token and returns a session.
- GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=google starts the Google redirect flow.
- PATCH /auth/v1/user updates the signed-in user, and converts anonymous users to email + password.
- POST /auth/v1/logout revokes the session behind a refresh token.
- GET /auth/v1/user returns the signed-in user, read from the bearer token.

The access token is HS256, signed with the project’s signing secret. Its sub claim is the user id, and that id becomes cubibase.user_id for Data API transactions. A table with a user column now has a real person behind every row policy check.

## Sessions that rotate and can be revoked

By default an access token lives for one hour and a refresh token for 30 days. Refreshing issues a new pair and retires the old refresh token. If a retired refresh token is presented again, CubiBase revokes the whole token family, so a stolen copy stops working.

Every Data API request checks that the session behind the token is still live. Revoking a session, or banning a user, takes effect on the next request, not when the access token expires.

## Anonymous users who become real accounts

Switch on Allow anonymous sign-ins in the project’s Providers settings and visitors can start using the app immediately: POST /auth/v1/signup/anonymous returns a full session for a user with no email or password. The user id is real, so rows they create under a user-column policy already belong to them.

When the visitor registers, the account is converted in place, not copied: PATCH /auth/v1/user with the anonymous bearer token plus an email and password keeps the same user id, sessions, metadata, and data. Linking Google with the anonymous bearer token does the same. In the Console, anonymous users carry an Anonymous badge and a dedicated filter.

## Google sign-in, configured in minutes

Google is a built-in OAuth/OIDC provider. Create a Web application OAuth client in the Google Cloud Console, register the redirect URI CubiBase shows you, and paste the Client ID and Client secret into Auth → Providers → Google. The secret is stored encrypted and never displayed again.

- Browser flow: GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=google&redirect_to=… returns the Google consent URL; after consent, CubiBase redirects to your allowlisted app URL with the session tokens in the URL fragment.
- Token flow: apps that already hold a Google ID token (Google Sign-In on mobile or web) POST it to /auth/v1/token?grant_type=id_token; CubiBase verifies the RS256 signature, issuer, audience, and expiry.
- Linking: send the end-user bearer token with either flow and the Google identity attaches to that user — the anonymous-to-Google upgrade path.
- Safety: redirect targets are checked against a per-project allowlist, OAuth states are hashed and single-use, and a verified Google email can attach to a matching existing account.

The step-by-step guide — what to click in the Google Cloud Console, where the redirect URI goes, and how your app reads the tokens — is in the docs.

## TOTP multi-factor, per project

Turn MFA on in the project’s auth settings and users can enroll an authenticator app: POST /auth/v1/factors returns a TOTP secret and URI, and POST /auth/v1/factors/verify confirms the first code. You can also make MFA required for the whole project.

When a user with a verified factor signs in, the password grant returns an MFA challenge instead of a session. The app posts the challenge id and the six-digit code to /auth/v1/token?grant_type=mfa and receives the session. Challenges expire after five minutes.

## Settings you control per project

- Signup and password sign-in can each be switched off.
- Anonymous sign-ins are opt-in: Allow anonymous sign-ins in Auth → Providers.
- Google sign-in is opt-in: enable it and store the OAuth Client ID and secret in Auth → Providers.
- Minimum password length defaults to 8 characters.
- Access token TTL defaults to 1 hour; refresh token TTL defaults to 30 days.
- MFA can be optional or required.
- Rate limits per project: 30 signups per hour and 30 sign-ins per minute per IP by default, adjustable.

These settings and the user directory are managed from the Console: Auth → Providers, Users, Sessions, Multi-factor, and Rate limits. Auth events are also written to the project’s logs schema, readable from the Console SQL editor.

## What email verification does today

By default, signup marks the email as verified immediately (autoconfirm). CubiBase does not send a confirmation email to your end users yet. If you turn autoconfirm off, new users start unverified. Keep that in mind when you design your onboarding.

## Already have an identity provider?

You can keep it. Configure the project with a JWKS URL, issuer, and audience, and CubiBase verifies RS256 tokens from that provider on every Data API request. CubiBase Auth and an external provider are alternatives; a project’s requests are checked against the provider configuration you set.

While building, a development token issuer can mint an HS256 token for a user id you choose, when that issuer is enabled. Google is built in as a social provider; other social providers and SAML are not available today.

## FAQ

**Where do my application users live?**

In the auth schema of your project’s own PostgreSQL database, in auth.users. Passwords are stored only as Argon2id hashes. Refresh tokens are stored as hashes too. Google identities are rows in auth.identities, linked to the same user table.

**Do I still need my own auth server?**

Not for email and password, anonymous sessions, or Google sign-in. Signup, sign-in, refresh, logout, Google OAuth, and TOTP MFA are served by the project host. You still build the screens in your app; CubiBase answers the HTTP calls.

**What happens to an anonymous user’s data when they register?**

Nothing is moved or lost. Conversion updates the same auth.users row in place: the user id stays, sessions keep working, metadata is merged, and rows written under that id remain theirs. The same applies when they link Google instead of setting a password.

**Where do I configure Google sign-in?**

Two places. In the Google Cloud Console: an OAuth consent screen and a Web application OAuth client whose Authorized redirect URI is the callback URL CubiBase displays. In the CubiBase Console: Auth → Providers → Google, where you enable the provider and paste the Client ID and Client secret. The docs walk through every click.

**Does CubiBase send verification emails to my users?**

Not yet. Autoconfirm marks new users verified at signup by default. If you disable it, new users start unverified. Google sign-in marks the email verified when Google reports it verified. Developer-account emails from the Console are a separate flow.

**What happens when a refresh token is stolen and reused?**

Refresh tokens rotate. When a token that was already replaced is presented again, CubiBase revokes the entire token family and the attacker’s session dies with it.

## Related

- [Security](https://cubibase.com/features/security) — How the JWT subject becomes a row policy.
- [REST API](https://cubibase.com/features/rest-api) — The calls that consume the access token.
- [Google setup guide](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/google) — Every step in the Google Cloud Console and the CubiBase Console.
- [Anonymous sign-ins](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/anonymous) — Enable the toggle, sign in visitors, convert them later.
- [Email and password](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/email-password) — Sign up a first user, then call a table.

# Your tables. Your APIs. Automatically.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/rest-api

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/rest-api.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Once you expose a table, CubiBase serves it at https://{slug}.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/{table}. You do not write a controller for that table. You do choose the operations. A new table starts unexposed, and a request still needs a publishable key plus an end-user JWT.

## At a glance

- **Instant CRUD** — GET lists rows, POST creates one, PATCH and DELETE address a primary key. No controller to write.
- **Explicit exposure** — Select, insert, update, and delete are separate switches. A new table starts unexposed; turning a switch off revokes the grant.
- **Filters and ordering** — column=op.value with nine operators, order on up to three columns, and limit up to 1000.
- **RPC for SQL functions** — Grant Data API EXECUTE and call POST /rest/v1/rpc/{name} with named arguments. Row-level security applies inside the function.
- **Two credentials** — The apikey header names the project; the bearer JWT names the user. A valid key alone is not enough.
- **Stable error codes** — 401 for missing or invalid credentials, 404 for unexposed tables, 405 for operations you did not turn on.

## The request CubiBase actually accepts

The host selects the project. The path selects the table. The apikey header must be an active publishable key for that project. Authorization must be a bearer JWT whose subject CubiBase can verify.

- GET /rest/v1/customers lists rows. GET /rest/v1/customers/{id} reads one row.
- POST creates a row and returns 201. PATCH and DELETE address one primary key.
- Filters use column=op.value. Operators are eq, neq, gt, gte, lt, lte, like, ilike, and is.
- order is column.asc or column.desc, with at most three columns. limit defaults to 20 and cannot exceed 1000.
- A list response is an object with a data array. A single row is an object with a data value.

## Exposure is explicit

Select, insert, update, and delete are separate switches. If select is off, GET is not offered for that table. The API role receives only the grants you turn on. Turning a switch off revokes that privilege.

This is the sense in which the API is automatic. CubiBase maps the exposed table to HTTP. It does not publish every table you create, and it does not invent relationships or nested resources.

## Your functions, callable too

Logic that spans tables belongs in a SQL function. Write it in the Console, grant Data API EXECUTE, and your app calls it at POST /rest/v1/rpc/{name} with a JSON object of named arguments. The call runs with the end user’s identity, so row-level security applies inside the function.

- POST /rest/v1/rpc/customer_count with { "plan_name": "pro" } returns { "data": 2 }.
- SETOF functions return an array; void returns null; the envelope is the same data field as table routes.
- Revoking EXECUTE removes the endpoint immediately. Private functions answer 404, like missing ones.

## Errors worth handling

- 401 missing_api_key or invalid_api_key when the publishable key is absent or wrong.
- 401 missing_end_user_token when the bearer token is absent.
- 404 when the host is not an active project, or the table is not available for that call.
- 405 method_not_allowed when that operation is not exposed.

## FAQ

**Is the path /v1/customers or /rest/v1/customers?**

The Data API path is /rest/v1/{table} on your project host, for example https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers.

**Can I select a subset of columns?**

Yes. The select query parameter takes a comma-separated list of one to 64 columns.

**Can my app run custom SQL logic?**

Through functions, not raw SQL. Create a function in the Console, grant Data API EXECUTE, and call POST /rest/v1/rpc/{name}. The SQL editor itself stays a Console tool.

## Related

- [Security](https://cubibase.com/features/security) — Why the key and the JWT do different jobs.
- [Calling functions (RPC)](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/rpc) — Arguments, result shapes, and overload rules.
- [PostgreSQL](https://cubibase.com/features/postgresql) — Where those rows actually live.
- [Data API docs](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api) — A worked example for the customers table.

title: See your data. Shape your database.
text:
# See your data. Shape your database.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/database-management

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/database-management.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

The Console is the developer view of a project database. You create tables, browse and edit rows, write row-level security policies, and manage functions, triggers, indexes, types, and views — all in the public schema. These are developer tools in the Console, separate from the Data API your application calls.

## At a glance

- **Tables and columns** — Up to 64 columns with nine PostgreSQL types and defaults like gen_random_uuid() and now().
- **Row browser** — Filter, select, and order with the same syntax as the Data API. Owners and admins edit rows; developers read.
- **Policies** — Write PostgreSQL policies with USING and WITH CHECK expressions for the API and Console roles.
- **Functions and triggers** — SQL or PL/pgSQL functions with overloads and SECURITY DEFINER, run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE.
- **Indexes, types, views** — Six index methods, enums and composite types, saved views, and materialized views with a refresh button.
- **Read-only SQL editor** — One statement, at most 200 rows, a short timeout. Inspect data here; change schema in the Database screens.

## Tables and columns

A new table needs a name, one primary key, and up to 64 columns. You can add a column later. You cannot add a primary key later, and you cannot drop the primary key or the user column used for row policies.

Supported types are uuid, text, integer, bigint, boolean, timestamptz, jsonb, numeric, and double precision. Defaults can be gen_random_uuid(), now(), true, or false.

## Rows, filters, and sorting

The row browser lists a table with the same filter, select, and order syntax as the Data API. Owners and admins can insert, update, and delete rows from the Console. A developer membership can read. These calls use the SQL role, so they are project-administration operations, not end-user requests.

## Policies, functions, triggers, indexes, types, views

The Database menu goes beyond tables. Every object you create lives in the public schema of your project database, owned by the project’s own DDL role. The platform schemas — auth, vault, logs — stay managed and out of reach.

- Policies: enable or disable Row Level Security per table, and write PostgreSQL policies with USING and WITH CHECK expressions for the API and Console roles.
- Functions: create and replace SQL or PL/pgSQL functions, with overloads, SECURITY DEFINER, and a Data API execute grant.
- Triggers: run a function automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE — before or after, per row or per statement, with WHEN conditions.
- Indexes: btree, hash, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, and BRIN; composite columns, expressions, partial filters, and unique indexes. Constraint-backed indexes are protected.
- Types: enums with ordered labels you can add and rename, and composite types for function returns.
- Views: saved SELECT queries, plus materialized views with a refresh button and a Data API select grant.

## The SQL editor stays read-only

- One statement, at most 8,000 characters.
- It must start with select, with, explain, show, values, or table.
- The transaction is read-only, with a statement timeout of a few seconds.
- The response includes at most 200 rows and says when the result was truncated.

Use the editor to inspect data. Use the Database screens when you need a new column, policy, function, or index.

## FAQ

**Can I paste a migration file into the SQL editor?**

No. The editor rejects anything that is not a single read-only statement. Schema changes go through the Database screens: tables, policies, functions, triggers, indexes, types, and views.

**Can I create objects in schemas other than public?**

No. The Database managers work only in the public schema of your project database. The auth, vault, and logs schemas are platform-managed and cannot be modified from the Console.

**Will the row browser show every end user’s rows?**

The Console uses the SQL role, whose table policy allows the developer to manage rows in the project. Application users are limited by the API role and the user-column policy. Those are different paths.

## Related

- [PostgreSQL](https://cubibase.com/features/postgresql) — How the project database is provisioned.
- [REST API](https://cubibase.com/features/rest-api) — Expose a table after you are ready for application traffic.
- [Policies](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/policies) — Write your own row-level security rules.
- [Functions and triggers](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions) — Database logic that runs where the data lives.
- [SQL editor](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/sql-editor) — The limits, with example queries.

title: Access you control. Data you protect.
text:
# Access you control. Data you protect.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/security

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/security.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

CubiBase separates project identity from user identity. The publishable key tells the Data API which project you are calling. The end-user JWT tells it which subject to apply. Row policies on the API role decide which rows that subject can touch. None of this is a certification, an SLA, or a promise that a mis-designed policy is safe.

## At a glance

- **Project isolation** — Each active project has its own database and roles. A request reaches only its own project’s database.
- **Key and token, different jobs** — The publishable key names the project and never authorizes a row. The bearer JWT names the user.
- **Forced Row Level Security** — Created tables have RLS enabled and forced. A user column binds the API role to cubibase.current_user_id().
- **Your own policies** — Write USING and WITH CHECK expressions per command, permissive or restrictive, validated before PostgreSQL sees them.
- **Live session checks** — Every request verifies the session is live and the user is not banned. Revocation takes effect on the next call.
- **Hardened Console session** — Argon2id developer passwords, HTTP-only cookies, a CSRF cookie, single-use email tokens, rotating refresh.

## Project isolation

Each active project has its own database and its own roles. The Data API will not serve a project that is not active, and a request on one project host cannot reach another project’s data. Your developer account and project settings are stored separately from project data.

## The key and the token do different jobs

Send the publishable key in the apikey header. It is meant to live with the client because it does not authorize rows. Treat it as a project credential anyway: revoke it if it leaks, and do not confuse it with a secret.

Send the user’s JWT as a bearer token. CubiBase Auth issues HS256 tokens signed with the project’s signing secret when your users sign up or sign in through /auth/v1. Alternatively, CubiBase accepts RS256 when you set a JWKS URL, issuer, and audience for your own identity provider. The verified subject is written to cubibase.user_id for that transaction.

For tokens that carry a session id, every request also checks that the session is still live and the user is not banned. A revoked session fails on the next call, even if the access token has not expired. A development issuer can still mint a token for a user id you choose while you are building.

The Console can also create a secret key with the prefix cb_sec_. That secret is returned once and stored as a hash. The Data API does not authenticate with it. Do not send it from a client in the expectation that it will return rows.

## Row Level Security

Tables created through CubiBase have Row Level Security enabled and forced. If you pass a text column as the user column, CubiBase creates a policy for the API role: a row is visible and writable only when that column equals cubibase.current_user_id(). If you skip the user column, the API role has no isolation policy of its own.

The SQL role, used by the Console, has a separate policy so the project developer can work with rows. Forcing RLS does not mean the Console is limited to a single end user.

Beyond the created policy, the Policies screen lets you write your own: USING and WITH CHECK expressions per command, permissive or restrictive, targeting the API role, the SQL role, or both. Expressions are validated as single expressions and checked against the table’s columns before PostgreSQL ever sees them.

## Your Console session

Developer passwords are hashed with Argon2id. The Console keeps the access and refresh tokens in HTTP-only cookies, so page scripts cannot read them. A CSRF cookie is readable by the Console’s own requests. Email verification and password reset use single-use tokens. Refresh tokens rotate.

## What this page does not claim

CubiBase has not published a compliance certification, a residency guarantee, or an uptime SLA. The public endpoints are served over HTTPS. You still choose the user column, the exposure flags, and how your app signs tokens.

## FAQ

**Can I rely on the publishable key as the only protection?**

No. The Data API rejects a call that has a valid key and no end-user token. You also need a row policy that matches the way your table stores the user id.

**Where are developer passwords stored?**

Only as Argon2id hashes, stored separately from your project data. This website never sees your password; you sign in on console.cubibase.com.

## Related

- [Authentication](https://cubibase.com/features/authentication) — Where the end-user JWT comes from.
- [REST API](https://cubibase.com/features/rest-api) — The headers and status codes your app will see.
- [Acceptable use](https://cubibase.com/acceptable-use) — The boundary for security testing.
- [Privacy draft](https://cubibase.com/privacy) — How account data and application data differ.

title: File storage inside every project.
text:
# File storage inside every project.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/storage

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/storage.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

CubiBase Storage keeps your files in private, encrypted object storage and the file catalog in your project’s PostgreSQL database. Apps upload directly with short-lived authorizations, every download is metered, and private buckets require a key, a user session, or a signed link.

## At a glance

- **Public and private buckets** — Per-bucket visibility, MIME allowlists, and size caps. Folders are path prefixes over opaque physical keys.
- **Direct uploads** — A presigned POST pinned to one upload and the exact size. The file goes straight from the client to storage.
- **Metered downloads** — Every download counts against bandwidth. Range requests are metered byte-accurately.
- **Signed share links** — A signed token scoped to a single object with a short expiry. Public objects also have a stable public URL.
- **Hard quotas** — Capacity checked atomically before any upload authorization. At a limit, uploads stop by default — metered additional usage is an explicit opt-in with a spending limit.
- **Durable object events** — Created, updated, and deleted events recorded with every catalog change, ready to trigger Functions.

## Public and private buckets

A bucket is a named container for objects, unique within the project. Each bucket is public or private, can cap the file size below the plan maximum, and can restrict uploads to an allowlist of MIME types such as image/* or application/pdf.

- Public means anonymous read-only access to published files. Uploads, overwrites, and deletions always require authorization.
- Private buckets require a project API key, an end-user session, or a short-lived signed download link.
- Folders are path prefixes, not real directories: images/avatar.png is a logical path, while the stored object uses an opaque generated key.
- Bucket metadata lives in a managed storage schema in the project database — customer code cannot read or write it directly.

## Direct uploads, verified completion

An upload takes three steps. Your client starts an upload session; CubiBase reserves the bytes against the project and account quotas and returns a short-lived presigned POST pinned to one upload and the exact declared size. The client posts the file directly to storage. Then the client completes the session: CubiBase checks the stored object’s exact size and MIME type, publishes it at its path, and turns the reservation into committed usage.

Completion is idempotent, expired sessions release their reservations automatically, and a failed upload never becomes a downloadable object or emits a creation event. Overwriting an existing path requires an explicit opt-in and accounts for the net change in bytes.

## Metered downloads and signed links

Every download — public or private, API or Console — counts against the account’s monthly bandwidth quota. HTTP Range requests are supported and metered byte-accurately; a canceled download counts only the bytes actually delivered. There are no unrestricted download URLs that could bypass the meter.

For sharing, CubiBase issues a signed download token scoped to a single object with a short expiry. Public objects also have a stable public URL.

## Quotas enforced on the server

Storage limits come from the same subscription as the rest of the platform, shared across your organization: Free includes 2 GB of object storage, Pro 100 GB, Business 250 GB, with 15 GB/500 GB/750 GB of monthly total bandwidth shared by API responses and file delivery (API bandwidth is a sublimit of that total) and a 50 MB/1 GB/5 GB maximum file size. Capacity is checked atomically before any upload authorization is issued, so concurrent uploads cannot race past it.

- At a storage limit, new uploads are blocked; downloads, deletions, and upgrades keep working.
- When bandwidth is exhausted, downloads are refused until the billing cycle resets; metadata management stays available.
- Downgrading below current usage preserves every file and blocks uploads until usage fits the new plan.
- No automatic overage charges: by default a quota is a hard stop, not a bill. Paid plans can opt in to metered additional usage with a spending limit.

## Durable object events and function triggers

Every finalized upload, overwrite, and deletion records a versioned storage.object.created, storage.object.updated, or storage.object.deleted event in the same database transaction as the catalog change. Events carry the project, bucket, object, path, size, and actor identity — never file contents or credentials.

CubiBase Functions consume these events through storage triggers: generate thumbnails, process PDFs, clean up expired files. Configure a bucket, event types, and an optional key prefix in the Console — no polling infrastructure of your own. Function-created objects count toward the same quotas through the same service, and invocation-depth tracking bounds recursive loops.

## FAQ

**Do storage credentials ever reach the client?**

No. Clients receive only a short-lived presigned POST for one upload with an exact size, or a signed download token for one object. The underlying storage blocks all public access.

**What happens to a file when I overwrite it?**

The new upload must explicitly opt in to overwriting. CubiBase verifies the new object before replacing the old one and adjusts usage by the net difference in bytes. A storage.object.updated event is recorded.

**Is storage isolated between projects?**

Yes. Stored objects are namespaced by project and bucket, the catalog lives in each project’s own database, and every request is resolved from the project host and credentials — never from a client-supplied project id.

## Related

- [Storage docs](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage) — Buckets, uploads, downloads, and quota errors with real API calls.
- [Security](https://cubibase.com/features/security) — Keys, JWTs, and the authorization model Storage reuses.
- [Pricing](https://cubibase.com/pricing) — Storage and bandwidth quotas on every plan.

title: Your code, next to your data.
text:
# Your code, next to your data.

Source: https://cubibase.com/features/functions

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/features/functions.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

CubiBase Functions run your TypeScript and JavaScript in an isolated, managed runtime. Four trigger types share one execution pipeline: HTTPS endpoints, committed database changes, storage object events, and cron schedules.

## At a glance

- **HTTPS endpoints** — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, and OPTIONS at /functions/{name}, with the exact raw body preserved for signature verification.
- **Database events** — After-commit INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE events captured atomically with your data change. A function failure never rolls back your transaction.
- **Storage events** — Object created, updated, and deleted events, filtered by bucket and key prefix. File contents never ride in the payload.
- **Cron schedules** — Standard cron expressions in UTC or a configured timezone, with last and next run visibility. Missed runs collapse into one catch-up run.
- **Gateway authentication** — JWT, public, secret API key, or internal-only access, enforced before your code runs. Payload signature verification is a separate setting.
- **Signed webhooks** — Built-in HMAC-SHA256 with replay protection, or verify Stripe and GitHub signatures yourself on the untouched body.
- **Immutable deployments** — Every deploy builds a new version. A failed build leaves the working version serving; activate an older version to roll back.
- **Eight templates** — Hello World, Stripe Webhook, GitHub Webhook, Send Email, OpenAI Proxy, Image Processing, Database Change Handler, and Scheduled Cleanup.
- **Execution history** — Trigger, version, duration, status, error category, and captured console output for every run, with filters and a delivery queue.
- **Encrypted secrets** — Secrets are encrypted at rest, never returned by read APIs, and redacted from logs. Functions get a short-lived, single-invocation credential.
- **Enforced quotas** — Invocations and GB-seconds metered per organization, shared across projects. At a limit, invocations are refused with 402 by default; paid plans can opt in to metered additional usage with a spending limit.
- **Durable delivery** — Async triggers deliver at least once, with durable retries and a queryable dead-letter queue. Deduplicate on the event id.

## Functions, not SQL functions

A CubiBase Function is application code you deploy from the Console: a default-exported async handler that receives the request or event and a context with scoped database, storage and environment access. It runs on Node.js 22 in a separate, isolated environment per project and function, with no platform credentials and no access to other projects.

This is different from PostgreSQL SQL functions, which live inside your project database and are managed under Database → SQL Functions. Both exist; they do different jobs. Database Event Triggers bridge them: a committed INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE can invoke a CubiBase Function asynchronously.

Execution is regional today. CubiBase does not offer globally distributed edge execution.

## Four ways to run

- HTTP: an HTTPS endpoint at https://{project}.api.cubibase.com/functions/{name}, supporting GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and OPTIONS, with the exact raw request body preserved for signature verification.
- Database: after-commit INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events on tables you subscribe to, captured atomically with your data change. A function failure never rolls back your transaction.
- Storage: object created, updated and deleted events from the existing Storage event stream, filtered by bucket and key prefix. Failed uploads never emit events; file contents never ride in the payload.
- Scheduled: standard cron expressions in UTC or a configured timezone, with last/next run visibility. Missed runs collapse into one catch-up run.

Database, storage and scheduled executions are asynchronous with at-least-once delivery, durable retries and a queryable dead-letter queue. Deduplicate on the event id — the templates show the pattern.

## Authentication and signed payloads

HTTP functions choose an authentication mode enforced by the gateway before your code runs: JWT (the default, using CubiBase Auth tokens), public, secret API key, or internal-only. Payload signature verification is a separate, independent setting.

- Built-in HMAC-SHA256: the gateway verifies the exact raw bytes with timestamp tolerance, constant-time comparison and single-use nonces (replay protection). Signing secrets are encrypted, shown once, and rotatable without dropped deliveries.
- Custom verification: Stripe, GitHub and other providers keep their own signature schemes. The function receives the untouched body and headers; the Stripe and GitHub templates verify them with constant-time checks.
- Secrets are encrypted at rest, never returned by read APIs, and redacted from logs. Functions reach your database and files through scoped CubiBase APIs with a short-lived, single-invocation credential — never a database password.

## Deployments that cannot break production

Every deploy builds an immutable version. Your code is bundled, never executed at build time, and imports are limited to Node built-ins plus a pinned dependency allowlist. A successful build atomically switches the active version; a failed build leaves the working version serving. Activate an older version to roll back.

## Start from working code

Eight versioned templates generate editable, functional code with the right trigger and security defaults: Hello World, Stripe Webhook, GitHub Webhook, Send Email, OpenAI Proxy, Image Processing, Database Change Handler and Scheduled Cleanup. The Stripe template verifies Stripe-Signature on the raw body, deduplicates deliveries, and walks you through the Dashboard configuration — it never claims the integration is connected until a signed test event succeeds.

## Every run is visible

Each invocation records its trigger, deployment version, duration, status, error category and captured console output — bounded, redacted and isolated per project. The Console shows execution history with filters, a delivery queue for async events, and per-function logs. Retention follows your plan.

## Quotas on every trigger

Functions use the same subscription as the rest of CubiBase. Function count, concurrent executions and schedules are limited per project; invocations and compute (GB-seconds) are metered per organization per billing cycle, shared across all projects — the same convention as bandwidth. Every trigger type passes the same atomic reservations; there is no side door. By default, at a limit invocations are refused, not billed as overage (paid plans can explicitly enable metered additional usage with a spending limit); exhausting compute also refuses invocations even if invocation capacity remains. The Console’s Usage page shows live consumption, warnings at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100%, and exceeded state; the pricing page lists the current plan values.

## FAQ

**Where does my function code actually run?**

In a managed Node.js 22 runtime, in an isolated environment per function, with no platform credentials and no access to other projects. Execution is regional.

**Can a database event function block or roll back a write?**

No — by design. Events are captured in the same transaction as your change but delivered only after commit, asynchronously. Use PostgreSQL constraints or native database triggers for rules that must block the write itself.

**Can I use npm packages?**

Imports are restricted to Node built-ins and a pinned allowlist (currently the official Stripe SDK). No build scripts run and no per-deploy npm install happens. The allowlist is versioned and will grow deliberately.

**Is this globally distributed like edge functions?**

No. Execution is regional, which is why the product is called Functions, not Edge Functions.

**What happens when I hit a quota?**

By default, new invocations are refused with a 402 until the cycle resets or you upgrade; async events retry with backoff and then dead-letter. Concurrency pressure returns 429 to HTTP callers. Nothing is silently over-billed — metered additional usage only applies when a paid organization explicitly enables it with a spending limit.

## Related

- [Functions docs](https://cubibase.com/docs/functions) — The programming model, triggers and worked examples.
- [Templates](https://cubibase.com/docs/functions/templates) — Eight starting points, including the Stripe webhook.
- [Quotas and metering](https://cubibase.com/docs/functions/quotas) — What is counted and the current plan values.
- [Storage](https://cubibase.com/features/storage) — The object events storage triggers consume.

title: CubiBase documentation
text:
# CubiBase documentation

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

CubiBase gives every project a PostgreSQL database, end-user authentication, and a REST API for the tables you expose. These docs cover the engine as it works today.

## What is CubiBase?

You create a project in the Console. CubiBase provisions a dedicated PostgreSQL database for it, and your application talks to that database over HTTPS — no server to run, no connection string to manage.

- A database per project. Ordinary PostgreSQL tables, plus managed `auth`, `logs`, and `vault` schemas.
- Auth for your users. Email + password, anonymous sign-ins, Google sign-in, and TOTP multi-factor, served at `/auth/v1`.
- REST for exposed tables. `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE` at `/rest/v1/{table}`, with filters, sorting, and pagination. Granted functions are callable at `/rest/v1/rpc/{name}`.
- S3-backed storage. Public and private buckets, direct uploads, signed links, and metered downloads at `/storage/v1`.
- Functions. TypeScript and JavaScript at `/functions/{name}`, plus database, storage, and cron triggers in an isolated runtime.
- A Console for you. Tables, rows, policies, SQL functions, triggers, indexes, types, views, a read-only SQL editor, functions, files, API keys, auth settings, and usage.

> **note**: Client SDKs are not published yet. Every example in these docs is a plain HTTP request you can send with `fetch`, `curl`, or any HTTP client.

## Your first request

Once a table is exposed, reading it is one request. The host selects the project, the `apikey` header identifies it, and the bearer token identifies the user. This example uses the fictional slug `example-project`.

**Request**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?plan=eq.pro&order=name.asc&limit=20
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

**200 · response**

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "8c1a0b2e-7d44-4a11-9c31-0b51a6e4d901",
      "name": "Mina Cho",
      "email": "mina@example.com",
      "plan": "pro",
      "owner_id": "user_mina"
    },
    {
      "id": "44ab91c3-0e55-4d72-b018-6f2c8a91bb70",
      "name": "Priya Shah",
      "email": "priya@example.org",
      "plan": "pro",
      "owner_id": "user_priya"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Pick your path

- [Quickstart](https://cubibase.com/docs/quickstart) From an empty account to a first authenticated query in five steps.
- [How CubiBase works](https://cubibase.com/docs/architecture) The two API surfaces, the project host, and what provisioning creates.
- [Authentication](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth) Sign users up, manage sessions, and add Google or MFA.
- [Data API](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api) Query and write rows with filters, sorting, and row policies.
- [Database objects](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/policies) Policies, functions, triggers, indexes, types, and views in the public schema.
- [Storage](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage) S3-backed files: buckets, direct uploads, signed links, and quotas.
- [Functions](https://cubibase.com/docs/functions) TypeScript/JavaScript on HTTP, database, storage, and cron triggers.

## What is documented here

These pages describe the engine that exists today: the Data API, CubiBase Auth, the Console tools, and the platform rules for quotas and inactivity. A full control-API reference and client libraries are not published yet — if a command is not in these docs, it is not a supported public interface.

## Additional resources

- [Quickstart](https://cubibase.com/docs/quickstart) Create a project, expose a table, call it.
- [Feature overview](https://cubibase.com/features) What a project includes, in product terms.
- [FAQ](https://cubibase.com/faq) Short answers to common questions.

# Quickstart

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/quickstart

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/quickstart.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Create a project, define a table, expose the operations you want, sign up a user, and call the Data API. About ten minutes, all HTTP.

## 1 · Create a project

1. **Register in the Console** — Create a developer account and verify your email address. Project creation requires a verified email.
2. **Create a project** — Pick a name and a slug. The slug becomes the first label of your API host: `{slug}.api.cubibase.com`.
3. **Wait for provisioning** — Provisioning is queued. The project page shows the status; wait until it reports active before creating tables.

**Provisioning state change, illustration.** Project example-project Provisioning → Active.

- Database example_project_db
- Roles ddl · api · sql · auth
- Schemas public · auth · vault · logs

Illustration of the state change. Creating a project queues the database; it exists when provisioning finishes.

> **important**: The database exists when provisioning finishes, not when you type the project name. Calls to a project that is not active return `404 project_not_found`.

## 2 · Define a table

In the Console, open your project and create a table. This guide uses a `customers` table:

**customers — example schema**

| Column | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `uuid` | Primary key, default `gen_random_uuid()` |
| `name` | `text` | Required |
| `email` | `text` | Required |
| `plan` | `text` | Required |
| `owner_id` | `text` | Set as the user column for row-level security |

Setting `owner_id` as the user column at creation time makes every row belong to the user whose JWT subject matches it. The policy is created with the table — you cannot attach it later.

> **tip**: Skip the user column only for tables every signed-in user may read and write, such as a shared product catalog.

## 3 · Expose the operations you want

New tables are not exposed. On the table screen, switch on the operations your app needs — here, `select` and `insert`. Leave `update` and `delete` off until you need them.

**customers · exposure illustration.** Operation switches: select (GET) on, insert (POST) on, update (PATCH) off, delete (DELETE) off.

Served at /rest/v1/customers for the operations you switched on. With everything off: The Data API treats this table as not found. Nothing is exposed.

Illustration. Toggles here do not change any real table.

## 4 · Sign up your first user

Copy the publishable key from the project’s API keys screen, then sign a user up. The response contains the `accessToken` your Data API calls need.

**Sign up · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/signup
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "mina@example.com",
  "password": "<USER_PASSWORD>"
}
```

> **note**: Email autoconfirm is on by default: the user is verified immediately and CubiBase does not send a confirmation email yet.

## 5 · Call the Data API

Send the publishable key in the `apikey` header and the user’s access token as the bearer token. With the `owner_id` policy in place, this user only sees their own rows.

**Request**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?plan=eq.pro&order=name.asc&limit=20
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

**200 · response**

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "8c1a0b2e-7d44-4a11-9c31-0b51a6e4d901",
      "name": "Mina Cho",
      "email": "mina@example.com",
      "plan": "pro",
      "owner_id": "user_mina"
    },
    {
      "id": "44ab91c3-0e55-4d72-b018-6f2c8a91bb70",
      "name": "Priya Shah",
      "email": "priya@example.org",
      "plan": "pro",
      "owner_id": "user_priya"
    }
  ]
}
```

> **tip**: Rows you insert should carry the user’s id in `owner_id`. The policy checks reads and writes: a row with someone else’s id is rejected with `403 forbidden`.

## Additional resources

- [Querying rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/querying) Filters, column selection, sorting, and pagination.
- [Sessions and tokens](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions) Refresh the session before the access token expires.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) How the user column becomes a PostgreSQL policy.

text:
# How CubiBase works

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/architecture

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/architecture.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Two HTTP surfaces, one database per project. The Console manages the project through the control API; your application calls the project host.

## The two surfaces

**How a request reaches the project database, illustration.** Developer → Console (tables · rows · SQL · keys) → Control plane / Control API (projects · schema · auth settings). Application → Your app (apikey + user JWT) → Project host (example-project.api.cubibase.com: /rest/v1 · /auth/v1 · /storage/v1 · /functions) → One project database, example_project_db (public · auth · storage · logs).

Illustration. The Console manages the project; your app calls the project host.

| Surface | Who calls it | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control API | The Console (your developer session) | Accounts, projects, tables, rows, SQL, API keys, auth settings, usage |
| Data API · `/rest/v1` | Your application | Reads and writes on the tables you expose |
| Auth API · `/auth/v1` | Your application | Sign-up, sign-in, sessions, Google, MFA |

> **important**: Your application should only call the project host. The control API paths the Console uses are not a public application interface.

## The project host

Every project gets a host of the form `https://{slug}.api.cubibase.com`. The engine resolves the project from the trusted `Host` header — it never consults `X-Forwarded-Host` — and validates the publishable key against that project.

**Example project**

| Piece | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Slug | `example-project` |
| API host | `https://example-project.api.cubibase.com` |
| Database | `example_project_db` |
| Data API base | `/rest/v1` |
| Auth API base | `/auth/v1` |

## What provisioning creates

Provisioning creates one PostgreSQL database and four login roles, all `NOSUPERUSER` and `NOBYPASSRLS`:

| Role | Used by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ddl` | Schema API | Creates and alters tables |
| `api` | Data API | Serves exposed tables, limited by grants and row policies |
| `sql` | Console | Row browser and the read-only SQL editor |
| `auth` | Auth API | Sign-up, sign-in, and sessions against the `auth` schema |

Alongside `public`, where your tables live, the database has managed schemas: `auth` (users, sessions, factors, identities), `logs` (request and auth events), `vault` (project secrets no request role can read), and `storage` (the bucket and object catalog, upload sessions, and object events for S3-backed file storage). Developer accounts live separately, in the platform metadata database.

## How a request is authorized

1. The `Host` header selects the project; the `apikey` header must be an active publishable key for it.
2. The bearer JWT is verified (HS256 for CubiBase Auth, or RS256 against your IdP’s JWKS). Its `sub` claim is the user id.
3. For session-bearing tokens, the engine checks the session is still live and the user is not banned.
4. The query runs as the API role with `cubibase.user_id` set to that subject, so row policies apply to every statement.

## Additional resources

- [API keys](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/api-keys) Publishable keys, secret keys, and rotation.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) The policy that turns a JWT subject into row access.
- [PostgreSQL feature page](https://cubibase.com/features/postgresql) The product view of database isolation.

title: Tables and columns

# Tables and columns

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Create tables from the Console. Every table is an ordinary PostgreSQL table in the public schema, with Row Level Security enabled from the start.

## The rules a table follows

- Names are lowercase: a letter first, then letters, digits, and underscores (up to 41 characters).
- Exactly one primary key column, chosen at creation. You cannot add or drop a primary key later.
- Up to 64 columns per table.
- Columns can be added and dropped later — except the primary key and the user column used for row policies.

> **important**: Decide the user column when you create the table: the ownership policy is created with it. To protect an existing table another way, write your own policy on the Policies screen.

## Column types

| Type | PostgreSQL type | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uuid` | `uuid` | Primary keys, references to user ids |
| `text` | `text` | Names, emails, the user column |
| `integer` | `integer` | Counters, small numbers |
| `bigint` | `bigint` | Large counters, external ids |
| `boolean` | `boolean` | Flags |
| `timestamptz` | `timestamptz` | Timestamps with time zone |
| `jsonb` | `jsonb` | Flexible structured data |
| `numeric` | `numeric` | Exact decimals, money |
| `double` | `double precision` | Floating-point measurements |

Columns are `NOT NULL` by default; mark a column nullable when it may be empty. Available defaults are `gen_random_uuid()`, `now()`, `true`, and `false`.

## A worked example

The `customers` table used throughout these docs:

**customers**

| Column | Type | Constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `uuid` | Primary key · default `gen_random_uuid()` |
| `name` | `text` | Not null |
| `email` | `text` | Not null |
| `plan` | `text` | Not null |
| `owner_id` | `text` | Not null · user column |

With `owner_id` set as the user column, the API role can only read and write rows whose `owner_id` equals the JWT subject of the caller. The Console keeps full access through a separate developer policy.

## Changing a table later

| Change | Supported? | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add a column | Yes | Table screen → add column (not as a primary key) |
| Drop a column | Yes | Except the primary key and the user column |
| Add a primary key | No | Create the table with the right key |
| Attach a user column | No | Recreate the table, or write an equivalent policy on the Policies screen |
| Run DDL in the SQL editor | No | The editor is read-only; use the table screen |

> **note**: A new table starts unexposed: the Data API treats it as not found until you turn on at least one operation.

## Additional resources

- [Exposing tables](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/exposure) Turn on the operations your app needs.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) What the user column actually creates.
- [Writing rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/writing) Insert, update, and delete over HTTP.
