# Exposing tables

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/exposure

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/exposure.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

A table is private until you expose it. Select, insert, update, and delete are separate switches, and each one maps to a real PostgreSQL grant.

## One switch per operation

**customers · exposure illustration.** Operation switches: select (GET) on, insert (POST) on, update (PATCH) off, delete (DELETE) off.

Served at /rest/v1/customers for the operations you switched on. With everything off: The Data API treats this table as not found. Nothing is exposed.

Illustration. Toggles here do not change any real table.

| Switch | HTTP | PostgreSQL grant to the API role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `select` | `GET /rest/v1/{table}` | `GRANT SELECT` |
| `insert` | `POST /rest/v1/{table}` | `GRANT INSERT` |
| `update` | `PATCH /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` | `GRANT UPDATE` |
| `delete` | `DELETE /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` | `GRANT DELETE` |

Turning a switch off revokes the grant immediately. A request for an operation that is not exposed returns `405 method_not_allowed`.

## Choosing what to expose

- Start with `select` only, and add write operations when a screen needs them.
- A shared catalog might expose `select` to everyone; a per-user table pairs writes with a user column.
- Exposure is not authorization by itself: every request still needs a publishable key and an end-user JWT.
- The Console row browser is unaffected — it uses the SQL role, not the API role.

> **warning**: Exposing a table without a user column means every signed-in user can use the exposed operations on every row. Add the policy unless the data is meant to be shared.

## Additional resources

- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) Limit rows per user, not just operations per table.
- [Data API overview](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api) The request shape behind every switch.

title: Row-level security
text:
# Row-level security

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Set a user column when you create a table and CubiBase writes the PostgreSQL policy for you: a row belongs to the user whose id it carries.

## The model

Every table created through CubiBase has Row Level Security enabled and forced. Two policies exist from the start, and the Policies screen lets you add, edit, or drop your own:

| Policy | Role | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developer policy | `sql` (Console) | Full access, so you can manage every row |
| Isolation policy | `api` (Data API) | Only rows where the user column equals the caller’s id |

The user column must be a `text` column on the new table — `owner_id` in these docs. Its value is compared to the verified JWT subject, which the engine sets as `cubibase.user_id` for the transaction.

## The policy CubiBase creates

For a table `customers` with user column `owner_id`, the isolation policy is equivalent to:

**SQL · created for you**

```sql
CREATE POLICY customers_api_isolation ON public.customers
  FOR ALL TO example_project_db_api
  USING (owner_id = cubibase.current_user_id())
  WITH CHECK (owner_id = cubibase.current_user_id());
```

- `USING` limits which rows the user can read, update, or delete.
- `WITH CHECK` limits which rows the user can insert or update into: writing someone else’s id fails with `403 forbidden`.
- The check runs inside PostgreSQL, not in application code you have to remember.

## From JWT to rows

1. The user signs in; the access token’s `sub` claim is their user id.
2. Your app sends the token as `Authorization: Bearer …` on a Data API call.
3. The engine verifies the token and sets `cubibase.user_id` for that transaction.
4. PostgreSQL applies the policy: the query only sees rows where `owner_id` matches.

> **tip**: Insert rows with the user’s id in the user column. A common pattern is to read the id from the signup response (or the token’s `sub`) and set it on every write.

## What the policy does not do

- It is per-row ownership, not roles or teams. For richer rules — statuses, teams, published rows — write your own policies on the Policies screen.
- The user-column flag itself only exists at creation; an existing table can get an equivalent rule as a hand-written policy.
- It does not replace exposure switches: an unexposed operation is refused before any row is touched.
- Anonymous users work exactly like registered users — their id is real, so their rows are theirs.

## Additional resources

- [Policies](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/policies) Write your own USING and WITH CHECK rules.
- [Tables and columns](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables) Where the user column is chosen.
- [Anonymous users](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/anonymous) Visitors get real ids, so their rows are protected too.
- [Security overview](https://cubibase.com/features/security) Keys, tokens, roles, and policies together.

title: Policies
text:
# Policies

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/policies

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/policies.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

The Policies screen manages Row Level Security on your tables: turn RLS on or off per table, and write your own PostgreSQL policies with USING and WITH CHECK expressions.

## How policies fit the role model

Every project has two query roles. The `api` role serves Data API requests and is subject to your policies. The `sql` role serves the Console (row browser, SQL editor) and normally has a permissive developer policy so you can manage every row.

| Target role | Who uses it | Typical policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `api` | Your application’s end users (Data API) | Restrict rows per user, per team, or per status |
| `sql` | You, in the Console | Full access for administration |

Tables created with a user column already carry an isolation policy for the `api` role. The Policies screen lists those policies alongside any you add, and lets you edit or drop them.

## Enabling and disabling RLS

- Each table row shows whether RLS is enabled and forced.
- Disabling RLS makes every grant effective for every row — the policies stay stored but stop being applied.
- FORCE RLS applies policies even to the table owner. CubiBase enables it with RLS so nothing slips past by ownership.

> **warning**: Turning RLS off on an exposed table removes row restrictions for every signed-in user. Keep it on unless the whole table is meant to be shared.

## Writing a policy

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Command | `ALL`, `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE` — which statements the policy governs |
| `USING` | Which existing rows are visible for SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE |
| `WITH CHECK` | Which new or updated rows are allowed for INSERT, UPDATE |
| Permissive | Permissive policies combine with OR; restrictive policies combine with AND |
| Roles | `api`, `sql`, or both |

Expressions are ordinary PostgreSQL boolean expressions. Reference the signed-in user with `cubibase.current_user_id()`, which returns the verified JWT subject for the request:

**Example · published notes are readable by everyone**

```text
-- Command: SELECT · Role: api · USING:
status = 'published' OR owner_id = cubibase.current_user_id()
```

**Example · users may only write their own rows**

```text
-- Command: INSERT · Role: api · WITH CHECK:
owner_id = cubibase.current_user_id()
```

- INSERT policies accept only WITH CHECK; SELECT and DELETE accept only USING.
- For ALL and UPDATE, omitting WITH CHECK reuses the USING expression as the write check.
- Expressions must be a single expression — stacked statements are rejected with `400 validation_error`.
- Bare column names are checked against the table, so a typo fails fast instead of at query time.

## Editing and dropping

- Editing expressions or roles uses ALTER POLICY in place.
- Changing the command or the permissive flag recreates the policy inside one transaction, so the table is never left unprotected mid-change.
- Dropping a policy takes effect immediately for new requests.

> **tip**: Test a policy from your app with a real end-user token. The Console row browser uses the sql role, so it will not show you what the api role sees.

## Additional resources

- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) The user-column policy created with each table.
- [Exposing tables](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/exposure) Grants decide the operation; policies decide the rows.
- [Views](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/views) Another way to shape what the API can read.

title: SQL Functions
text:
# SQL Functions

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Create, edit, and replace SQL or PL/pgSQL functions in the public schema from the Console. Functions power triggers, encapsulate queries, and can be granted to the Data API role. These are PostgreSQL functions — for TypeScript/JavaScript code in the managed runtime, see the CubiBase Functions docs.

## Creating a function

The editor takes a name, an argument list, a return type, and a body. Bodies can contain multiple statements — unlike the SQL editor, a function body is a program, not a single query.

| Option | Values | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Language | `sql`, `plpgsql` | SQL for single queries; PL/pgSQL for logic and loops |
| Volatility | `VOLATILE`, `STABLE`, `IMMUTABLE` | Tell the planner how the function behaves |
| Security | `INVOKER`, `DEFINER` | DEFINER runs with the function owner’s rights |
| Strict | on / off | STRICT returns NULL immediately when any argument is NULL |
| Returns set | on / off | `SETOF` for functions that return multiple rows |
| Replace | on / off | `CREATE OR REPLACE` keeps existing grants |

**Example · PL/pgSQL**

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION public.customer_count(plan_name text)
RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql
STABLE
SECURITY INVOKER
SET search_path = public, pg_catalog
AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (SELECT count(*) FROM public.customers WHERE plan = plan_name);
END;
$$;
```

Every function is created with `SET search_path = public, pg_catalog`, so name resolution cannot be hijacked by objects in other schemas — important for SECURITY DEFINER functions.

## Overloads and dropping

- PostgreSQL identifies a function by name plus argument types. Two functions named `search` with different argument types can coexist.
- When you drop (or toggle API access on) an overloaded name, the Console asks which signature you mean — pass the argument types, e.g. `id uuid` vs `term text`.
- Replacing a function keeps its grants; dropping it removes them.

## Editing a function

Every function you created has an Edit button. It opens the same form prefilled with the current definition and saves with `CREATE OR REPLACE`, so existing grants and dependent triggers or views keep working.

- Editable: the body, argument defaults, volatility, security (INVOKER/DEFINER), STRICT, and the Data API grant.
- Fixed: the name, argument names/types/modes, return type, and language — PostgreSQL identifies a function by that signature and cannot change it in place. To change the signature, create a new function and drop the old one.
- Replacing keeps EXECUTE grants; dropping removes them.

> **note**: Extension functions cannot be edited — see below. Only functions you created are editable.

## Extension functions are read-only

Enabling an extension (Database → Extensions, e.g. `pgcrypto` or `pg_trgm`) installs its functions into the public schema. Those functions belong to the extension, not to you:

- Hidden by default: the Functions screen lists only your own functions. Tick “Show extension functions” to see the rest, marked with an `extension: pgcrypto` badge.
- Read-only: they cannot be edited, replaced, or dropped — the API refuses with `403 extension_function`. PostgreSQL itself also refuses to drop a function an extension depends on.
- They leave only with their extension: disable it on the Extensions screen and its functions disappear together.
- You can still grant or revoke Data API EXECUTE on them — that is how you expose e.g. `gen_random_uuid()` over RPC without writing a wrapper.

> **note**: The lock survives backups: restoring a project hands your objects back to your project role but never extension members, so a restored database cannot be used to rewrite extension internals.

## Data API execute permission

Functions are private by default: the Console’s `sql` role can run them, the `api` role cannot. The Data API execute switch maps to a real grant:

**SQL · what the switch runs**

```sql
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.customer_count(text) TO example_project_db_api;
-- off:
REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.customer_count(text) FROM example_project_db_api;
```

With the grant on, the function is callable from your app at `POST /rest/v1/rpc/{name}` on the project host, with the publishable key and the end-user JWT. The body is a JSON object of named arguments; the call runs with the caller’s identity, so RLS applies to SECURITY INVOKER functions.

**RPC · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/rpc/customer_count
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "plan_name": "pro" }
```

> **note**: The grant covers the function itself. Tables the body reads still need their own grants for the api role — expose them in the Console, or the call fails with 403. See Calling functions (RPC) for result shapes, overloads, and errors.

## SECURITY DEFINER, carefully

- A DEFINER function runs with its owner’s privileges, so it can bypass the caller’s RLS policies. That is the point — and the risk.
- Grant EXECUTE to the api role only when the function is meant to expose that capability.
- Validate arguments inside the function; a DEFINER function is a door through your policies.

> **warning**: A SECURITY DEFINER function granted to the api role can read or write rows the caller’s policies would block. Review the body before enabling Data API execute.

## Additional resources

- [Calling functions (RPC)](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/rpc) Call a granted function from your app over the Data API.
- [Triggers](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/triggers) Run a function automatically on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE.
- [Types](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/types) Enums and composites for arguments and return values.
- [SQL editor](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/sql-editor) Call your function with SELECT to test it.
- [CubiBase Functions](https://cubibase.com/docs/functions) TypeScript/JavaScript in the managed runtime — a different feature.

title: Triggers
text:
# Triggers

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/triggers

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/triggers.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Execute a function automatically when rows change. Triggers fire on INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE, before or after the event, per row or per statement.

## The shape of a trigger

| Choice | Values | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timing | `BEFORE`, `AFTER` | BEFORE can modify the row being written; AFTER sees the final state |
| Events | `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` | Combine several events in one trigger |
| Level | `ROW`, `STATEMENT` | ROW fires per affected row; STATEMENT once per query |
| Update of | column list | Fire only when specific columns are updated |
| WHEN | boolean expression | A row-level condition, e.g. `NEW.plan <> OLD.plan` |
| Function | a public trigger function | Must return `trigger` |

- TRUNCATE triggers must be FOR EACH STATEMENT — there are no rows to iterate.
- WHEN conditions require FOR EACH ROW.
- INSTEAD OF triggers apply to views and are not offered on tables.

## The trigger function

A trigger calls a function that returns `trigger`. Create it on the Functions screen (there is a trigger template), then pick it here. Inside the body, `NEW` is the row being written and `OLD` the row being replaced or removed.

**Example · stamp updated_at on every update**

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION public.set_updated_at()
RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := now();
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;
```

**SQL · what the Console creates**

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER customers_set_updated_at
BEFORE UPDATE ON public.customers
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION public.set_updated_at();
```

> **tip**: A BEFORE INSERT trigger can fill server-side fields — return NEW with the fields set and every writer gets them, including the Data API.

## Enabling, disabling, dropping

- The Triggers screen groups triggers by table and shows timing, events, level, function, and enabled state.
- Disabling a trigger keeps its definition but stops it firing — useful while backfilling data.
- Dropping the trigger does not drop the function; other triggers may still use it.
- Triggers run inside the writing transaction: if the function raises, the whole write is rolled back.

> **warning**: Trigger functions run with the privileges of the writing role and are not stopped by RLS on other tables they touch. Keep trigger bodies small and reviewed.

## Additional resources

- [Functions](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions) Where trigger functions are written and replaced.
- [Tables and columns](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables) The tables triggers attach to.
- [Writing rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/writing) The writes that fire your triggers.

title: Indexes
text:
# Indexes

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/indexes

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/indexes.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Speed up the queries your app actually runs. Create btree, hash, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, and BRIN indexes on public tables — single-column, composite, expression, or partial.

## Choosing a method

| Method | Good for |
| --- | --- |
| `btree` | Equality and range queries, sorting — the default and the only unique-capable method |
| `hash` | Equality-only lookups |
| `gin` | jsonb containment, arrays, full-text search |
| `gist` | Geometry, ranges, nearest-neighbour search |
| `spgist` | Partitioned data like points and text prefixes |
| `brin` | Very large tables whose physical order matches the column (e.g. timestamps) |

The Indexes screen lists every index in the public schema with its method, columns or expression, uniqueness, and size on disk.

## Composite, expression, and partial indexes

- Composite: pick up to 16 columns, each with ASC/DESC and optional NULLS FIRST/LAST. Column order matters — put the most-filtered column first.
- Expression: index a computed value, e.g. `lower(email)`, when your queries filter on that expression.
- Partial: add a WHERE filter, e.g. `status = 'active'`, to index only the rows you query.
- Unique: btree only; enforces uniqueness like a constraint.

**Examples · what the Console creates**

```sql
CREATE INDEX customers_plan_name ON public.customers (plan, name);

CREATE INDEX customers_email_lower ON public.customers (lower(email));

CREATE INDEX customers_active ON public.customers (owner_id)
WHERE status = 'active';

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_unique ON public.customers (email);
```

> **note**: Index creation on a large table takes a lock while it builds. Create indexes before the table grows, or during a quiet period.

## Constraint-backed indexes are protected

- Primary keys and unique constraints own their indexes. The screen marks them and refuses to drop them — dropping the index would drop the constraint’s enforcement.
- Ordinary indexes can be dropped at any time; queries fall back to sequential scans.
- Every index costs write speed and storage. Watch the size column and drop indexes your queries no longer use.

## Additional resources

- [Querying rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/querying) The filters and sorts your indexes should serve.
- [SQL editor](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/sql-editor) Run EXPLAIN to confirm the planner uses your index.
- [Tables and columns](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables) Where the primary key index comes from.

title: Types
text:
# Types

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/types

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/types.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Define custom enum and composite types in the public schema. Enums give a column a fixed vocabulary; composites bundle fields into one value for functions and PL/pgSQL.

## Enum types

An enum is an ordered list of labels. Create one with up to 256 labels, then use it as a column type in the SQL your functions and views run, or as a function argument or return type.

**Example · what the Console creates**

```sql
CREATE TYPE public.customer_plan AS ENUM ('free', 'pro', 'business');
```

| Change | Supported? | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add a label | Yes | At the end, or BEFORE/AFTER an existing label |
| Rename a label | Yes | Existing rows keep their value; the label text changes |
| Remove a label | No | PostgreSQL cannot drop enum values; recreate the type |
| Reorder labels | Only via add position | Use BEFORE/AFTER when adding |

> **tip**: Enum order is real: ORDER BY on an enum column sorts by label position, not alphabetically. Add labels in the order you want them sorted.

## Composite types

A composite is a named row shape — up to 64 attributes, each with a name and a type. Composites are useful as function return types (especially SETOF) and inside PL/pgSQL.

**Example · what the Console creates**

```sql
CREATE TYPE public.plan_summary AS (plan text, customers bigint);

CREATE FUNCTION public.plan_counts()
RETURNS SETOF public.plan_summary
LANGUAGE sql STABLE
AS $$
  SELECT plan, count(*) FROM public.customers GROUP BY plan;
$$;
```

## Rules and limits

- Names follow the same rule as tables: a lowercase letter first, then letters, digits, and underscores.
- Attribute and argument types can be built-ins (`text`, `numeric(10,2)`, `timestamptz`), arrays (`text[]`), or your own public types (`public.customer_plan`).
- Types referenced by columns, functions, or views cannot be dropped until those dependents are removed — the error is `409 object_in_use`.
- Platform schemas are off limits: you cannot create types in, or reference types from, auth, vault, logs, or cubibase.

## Additional resources

- [Functions](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions) Where custom types are most useful.
- [Tables and columns](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables) The built-in column types.
- [Views](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/views) Queries that can return your types.

title: Views
text:
# Views

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/views

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/views.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Save a SELECT as a view, or cache it as a materialized view. Views shape what readers see — joins, aggregates, renamed columns — without copying data.

## Creating a view

A view is one SELECT (or WITH … SELECT) query stored under a name. Querying the view runs the query against live data. The editor accepts a single statement up to 16,000 characters.

**Example · what the Console creates**

```sql
CREATE VIEW public.active_customers AS
SELECT id, name, plan
FROM public.customers
WHERE status = 'active';
```

- Standard views can be replaced in place (CREATE OR REPLACE) as long as column names and types stay compatible.
- Views over RLS-protected tables respect the querying role’s policies: the api role sees only the rows its policies allow.
- The Console lists each view with its definition and columns.

## Materialized views

A materialized view runs the query once and stores the result. Reads are fast and constant; the data is a snapshot until you refresh. CubiBase creates them WITH DATA, so they are usable immediately.

|  | View | Materialized view |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data freshness | Always live | As of the last refresh |
| Read cost | Runs the query each time | Reads stored rows |
| Replace in place | Yes | No — drop and recreate |
| Refresh button | — | Yes: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW |

> **note**: Refresh is manual in this release — press Refresh on the view (or call the control route) when you want new numbers. A refresh rebuilds the whole snapshot.

## The Data API select switch

Like tables, views start private. The Data API select switch grants SELECT on the view to the `api` role, so queries executed as that role — inside functions or other views — can read it. Turning the switch off revokes the grant immediately.

> **note**: The Data API serves tables at /rest/v1 in this release; views are not yet addressable as REST resources. Read a view from the SQL editor, or wrap it in a function.

> **warning**: A view can aggregate or join across rows a caller could not read directly. Grant select only when the combined result is meant to be visible, or add a WHERE on cubibase.current_user_id() inside the view.

## Additional resources

- [SQL editor](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/sql-editor) Read your views with a SELECT.
- [Policies](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/policies) Row rules that views inherit from their tables.
- [Indexes](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/indexes) Speed up the queries inside your views.

title: SQL editor
text:
# SQL editor

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/database/sql-editor

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/sql-editor.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Inspect your database with one read-only SQL statement at a time. The editor is for reading; schema changes go through the Database screens — tables, policies, functions, triggers, indexes, types, and views.

## The limits

| Rule | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Statements per run | Exactly one |
| Length | At most 8,000 characters |
| Allowed prefixes | `select`, `with`, `explain`, `show`, `values`, `table` |
| Transaction | Read-only, on the SQL role |
| Statement timeout | 3 seconds |
| Rows returned | At most 200; the response says when it was truncated |

> **important**: The editor will not create a table, add a column, or write a row. Anything that is not a single read-only statement is rejected with `400 invalid_sql`. Schema changes go through the Database screens.

## Useful queries

**Count rows per plan**

```sql
SELECT plan, count(*) AS customers
FROM public.customers
GROUP BY plan
ORDER BY customers DESC;
```

**Inspect your end users**

```sql
SELECT email, is_anonymous, email_verified_at, last_sign_in_at
FROM auth.users
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

The SQL role can read the managed `auth` and `logs` schemas, so the editor is also how you inspect users, sessions, and request logs. The `vault` schema is not readable from it.

## The response shape

**Result · trimmed**

```json
{
  "columns": ["plan", "customers"],
  "rows": [{ "plan": "pro", "customers": 2 }],
  "truncated": false,
  "rowCount": 2,
  "durationMs": 4,
  "readOnly": true,
  "maxRows": 200
}
```

## Additional resources

- [Tables and columns](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/tables) Where schema changes actually happen.
- [Functions](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions) Test your functions here with SELECT.
- [Sessions and tokens](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions) What the auth tables contain.

title: Data API overview
text:
# Data API overview

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Every exposed table is served at /rest/v1/{table} on your project host. Two headers on every request: the publishable key and the user’s JWT.

## The request shape

| Piece | Value | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host | `https://{slug}.api.cubibase.com` | Selects the project |
| Path | `/rest/v1/{table}` | Selects the exposed table |
| `apikey` header | Publishable key (`cb_pub_…`) | Identifies the project credential |
| `Authorization` header | `Bearer <USER_JWT>` | Identifies the end user |

**Request**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?plan=eq.pro&order=name.asc&limit=20
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

**200 · response**

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "id": "8c1a0b2e-7d44-4a11-9c31-0b51a6e4d901",
      "name": "Mina Cho",
      "email": "mina@example.com",
      "plan": "pro",
      "owner_id": "user_mina"
    },
    {
      "id": "44ab91c3-0e55-4d72-b018-6f2c8a91bb70",
      "name": "Priya Shah",
      "email": "priya@example.org",
      "plan": "pro",
      "owner_id": "user_priya"
    }
  ]
}
```

> **note**: The publishable key alone is not enough. A request without a bearer token fails with `401 missing_end_user_token`, even with a valid key.

## Response envelope

Every successful response wraps its payload in a `data` field. Lists return an array; single rows and writes return one object.

| Call | Status | `data` contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /rest/v1/{table}` | `200` | An array of rows (possibly empty) |
| `GET /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` | `200` | One row object |
| `POST /rest/v1/{table}` | `201` | The inserted row, all columns |
| `PATCH /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` | `200` | The updated row, all columns |
| `DELETE /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` | `200` | The deleted row, all columns |
| `POST /rest/v1/rpc/{function}` | `200` | The function result: a value, an object, or an array |

## Errors

Errors are JSON objects with a stable `code`, a human `message`, and a `requestId` you can match against the project logs.

**401 · missing bearer token**

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "missing_end_user_token",
    "message": "An end-user bearer token is required",
    "requestId": "req_example"
  }
}
```

| Status | Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401` | `missing_api_key` / `invalid_api_key` | The publishable key is absent or wrong |
| `401` | `missing_end_user_token` / `invalid_token` | The bearer JWT is absent or fails verification |
| `404` | `not_found` | Unknown table, unexposed table, or missing row |
| `405` | `method_not_allowed` | That operation is not exposed for the table |

## What the API does not do

- No joins or nested resources: one table request addresses one table. Logic that spans tables belongs in a function, called over RPC.
- No bulk writes: `POST` inserts one row; `PATCH` and `DELETE` address one primary key.
- No arbitrary SQL from the application — the SQL editor is a Console tool. Functions you write and grant are the supported way to run custom logic.
- Tables with composite primary keys are not served by the row-by-id routes.

## Additional resources

- [Querying rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/querying) Filters, select, order, limit, offset.
- [Writing rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/writing) Insert, update, delete, and constraint errors.
- [Calling functions (RPC)](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/rpc) Run your SQL functions from the app.
- [Error codes](https://cubibase.com/docs/reference/errors) The full list, with causes and fixes.

title: Querying rows
text:
# Querying rows

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/querying

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/querying.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Filter with column=op.value, pick columns with select, sort with order, and page with limit and offset. All of it in the query string.

## Filters

Any query parameter that is not reserved (`select`, `order`, `limit`, `offset`) is a filter: `column=op.value`. Multiple filters combine with AND.

**Operators**

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `eq` | Equals | `plan=eq.pro` |
| `neq` | Not equals | `plan=neq.free` |
| `gt` / `gte` | Greater than (or equal) | `age=gte.18` |
| `lt` / `lte` | Less than (or equal) | `price=lt.100` |
| `like` | Pattern match (case-sensitive) | `name=like.M%25` |
| `ilike` | Pattern match (case-insensitive) | `name=ilike.m%25` |
| `is` | `null`, `true`, or `false` | `archived_at=is.null` |

**Pro customers whose name starts with M**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?plan=eq.pro&name=ilike.m%25
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

> **tip**: URL-encode the `%` wildcard as `%25` in like/ilike patterns. Values are always bound as parameters — never concatenated into SQL.

## Choosing columns

`select` takes a comma-separated list of 1 to 64 columns. Without it, every column is returned.

**Only names and emails**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?select=name,email
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

## Sorting

`order` takes `column.asc` or `column.desc`, up to three columns separated by commas.

**Newest plans first, then name**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?order=plan.desc,name.asc
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

## Pagination

| Parameter | Default | Maximum | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `limit` | `20` | `1000` | Rows per page |
| `offset` | `0` | `100000` | Rows to skip |

**Page 3, 25 rows per page**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers?order=name.asc&limit=25&offset=50
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

> **note**: Always pair pagination with a stable `order`. Without it, PostgreSQL does not guarantee row order between pages.

## Reading one row

`GET /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` reads a single row by primary key. A missing row — or one the user’s policy hides — returns `404 not_found`.

**One customer**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers/8c1a0b2e-7d44-4a11-9c31-0b51a6e4d901
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

## Additional resources

- [Writing rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/writing) The other half of the API.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) Why a query may return fewer rows than exist.

title: Writing rows
text:
# Writing rows

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/writing

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/writing.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

POST inserts one row, PATCH updates one row by primary key, DELETE removes it. Each returns the affected row with every column.

## Insert a row

`POST /rest/v1/{table}` with a JSON object of column values. Columns with defaults can be omitted. The response is `201` with the full inserted row.

**Insert · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "Mina Cho",
  "email": "mina@example.com",
  "plan": "pro",
  "owner_id": "<USER_ID>"
}
```

> **important**: On a table with a user column, set that column to the calling user’s id (the JWT `sub`). Writing another user’s id fails the policy’s `WITH CHECK` with `403 forbidden`.

## Update a row

`PATCH /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` with the fields to change. Only the listed columns are touched; the response is the full updated row.

**Update · request**

```http
PATCH https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers/8c1a0b2e-7d44-4a11-9c31-0b51a6e4d901
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "plan": "team"
}
```

## Delete a row

`DELETE /rest/v1/{table}/{id}` removes the row and returns it in `data`. A row that does not exist — or is hidden by the user’s policy — returns `404 not_found`.

**Delete · request**

```http
DELETE https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers/8c1a0b2e-7d44-4a11-9c31-0b51a6e4d901
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

## Constraint errors

PostgreSQL constraints surface as stable error codes, so your app can react without parsing messages:

| Status | Code | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `409` | `conflict` | Unique constraint violated (e.g. duplicate email) |
| `400` | `not_null_violation` | A required column was omitted |
| `409` | `foreign_key_violation` | A referenced row does not exist |
| `400` | `check_violation` | A value failed a check constraint |
| `400` | `invalid_input` | A value does not fit the column type |
| `403` | `forbidden` | The row policy rejected the write |

> **note**: Bodies are limited to 64 fields, and row ids to 200 characters. `PATCH` and `DELETE` require a table with a single primary key column.

## Additional resources

- [Querying rows](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/querying) Read back what you wrote.
- [Error codes](https://cubibase.com/docs/reference/errors) Every code the engine can return.

title: Calling functions (RPC)
text:
# Calling functions (RPC)

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/rpc

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api/rpc.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

A function you grant to the Data API role is callable at POST /rest/v1/rpc/{name}. Same host, same publishable key, same end-user JWT. Arguments are a JSON object; the result comes back in data.

## The call

Write the function in the Console (Database, Functions), then switch on Grant Data API EXECUTE. The function is then served on the project host:

**RPC · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/rpc/customer_count
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "plan_name": "pro"
}
```

**200 · response**

```json
{
  "data": 2
}
```

The body is a JSON object keyed by parameter name. Values are bound as parameters and cast to the declared types, so "42" works for an integer and a JSON object feeds a jsonb parameter. Omit a key to use the parameter default; send {} (or no body) for a function without arguments.

> **note**: Only POST is served. A function that writes rows is still a POST — the method selects the call, not the effect. Statements run with the api pool’s 8-second timeout.

## What data contains

| Return type | `data` | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scalar (`integer`, `text`, `jsonb`, …) | The value itself | `{ "data": 2 }` |
| `SETOF` a scalar | An array of values | `{ "data": ["a-note", "b-note"] }` |
| `SETOF` a table or composite | An array of row objects | `{ "data": [{ "id": "…", "body": "…" }] }` |
| Composite / OUT parameters | One row object | `{ "data": { "total": 12, "mine": 3 } }` |
| `void` | `null` | `{ "data": null }` |

Results are JSON: bigint and numeric arrive as JSON numbers, timestamps as ISO strings. A set-returning function is capped at 10000 rows per call; page inside the function with arguments when you need more.

## Identity and row-level security

The call runs as the api role with cubibase.user_id set to the JWT subject, exactly like a table request. A SECURITY INVOKER function sees only the rows the caller’s policies allow:

**A function that respects RLS**

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION public.my_note_bodies()
RETURNS SETOF text
LANGUAGE sql
STABLE
SECURITY INVOKER
SET search_path = public, pg_catalog
AS $$
  SELECT body FROM public.notes ORDER BY body;
$$;
```

Two users calling my_note_bodies get two different arrays. SECURITY DEFINER runs as the function owner instead and can bypass the caller’s policies — grant it deliberately and validate arguments inside the body.

> **important**: EXECUTE on the function is not a grant on the tables it reads. The api role still needs SELECT (or write) privileges on those tables — expose the table in the Console, or the call fails with 403 forbidden. RLS then narrows the rows per user.

## Overloads and defaults

- Parameters are matched by name. Keys you send must exist on the function; required parameters must be present or have defaults.
- When several overloads accept the same keys, an exact match wins. A tie answers 300 ambiguous_function with the candidate signatures in details.
- Functions with unnamed parameters cannot be called with a JSON object; name the parameters in the Console.
- Defaults are applied by PostgreSQL, so the function body sees the same values as a direct SQL call.

## Errors

| Status | Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `401` | `missing_api_key` / `missing_end_user_token` | Same credential rules as table routes |
| `404` | `not_found` | No such function, no EXECUTE grant, or no overload matches the argument names |
| `400` | `invalid_body` | Body is not an object, or a value does not fit the parameter type |
| `403` | `forbidden` | A policy or a missing table grant blocked the function body |
| `300` | `ambiguous_function` | Several overloads match; details lists the signatures |
| `408` | `statement_timeout` | The function ran past the statement timeout |
| `413` | `result_too_large` | A set-returning function produced more than 10000 rows |

> **note**: Constraint failures inside the function surface with the same codes as table writes: conflict, foreign_key_violation, check_violation. RPC calls appear in the project request logs with the argument names and the user id.

## Additional resources

- [Functions](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/functions) Writing and granting functions in the Console.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) The policies an INVOKER function runs under.
- [API routes](https://cubibase.com/docs/reference/routes) Every route on the project host.
