text:
# Authentication overview

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

CubiBase Auth runs on your project host under /auth/v1. Users live in your project’s database, and the access token they receive is the JWT your Data API calls use.

## How it fits together

**Sign-up flow, illustration.** Your app (email + password) → POST /auth/v1/signup → CubiBase Auth (Argon2id hash) → INSERT auth.users → Your database (example_project_db). Response: 201 · session with accessToken, refreshToken, expiresIn: 3600.

Illustration. Sign-up returns the JWT your Data API calls use.

- Users are rows in `auth.users` inside your project’s PostgreSQL database — not a shared directory.
- Passwords are stored only as Argon2id hashes; refresh tokens are stored as hashes too.
- The `accessToken` is an HS256 JWT whose `sub` is the user id. Send it as the bearer token on Data API calls.
- A table with a user column filters rows by that id automatically.

## Sign-in methods

- [Email and password](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/email-password) Sign up, sign in, and the password rules.
- [Anonymous users](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/anonymous) Let visitors in first; convert them in place later.
- [Google sign-in](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/google) OAuth redirect flow and ID-token flow, step by step.
- [Multi-factor (TOTP)](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/mfa) Authenticator apps, challenges, and required MFA.

Already have an identity provider? Configure the project to verify its RS256 tokens instead — see External identity providers.

## The endpoints at a glance

| Endpoint | Purpose | Bearer token? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /auth/v1/signup` | Create a user, return a session | No |
| `POST /auth/v1/signup/anonymous` | Create an anonymous session | No |
| `POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=password` | Sign in | No |
| `POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token` | Refresh a session | No |
| `POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=mfa` | Complete an MFA challenge | No |
| `POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=id_token` | Verify a Google ID token | Optional (links) |
| `GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=google` | Start the Google flow | Optional (links) |
| `GET /auth/v1/callback` | Google redirects back here | No |
| `POST /auth/v1/logout` | Revoke a session | No |
| `GET /auth/v1/user` | Read the signed-in user | Yes |
| `PATCH /auth/v1/user` | Update the user; convert anonymous | Yes |
| `POST /auth/v1/factors` | Enroll a TOTP factor | Yes |
| `POST /auth/v1/factors/verify` | Confirm the first code | Yes |
| `DELETE /auth/v1/factors/{factorId}` | Remove a factor | Yes |

> **note**: Every endpoint requires the `apikey` header with the project’s publishable key — the same key as the Data API. The callback is the exception: Google’s redirect carries no headers, so the single-use state is its security boundary.

## Project settings

All of this is configured per project in Console → Auth: providers, password rules, token lifetimes, MFA, rate limits, the user directory, and sessions.

| Setting | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Signup enabled | On |
| Password sign-in enabled | On |
| Minimum password length | 8 characters |
| Email autoconfirm | On (no confirmation email is sent yet) |
| Access token lifetime | 1 hour |
| Refresh token lifetime | 30 days |
| Anonymous sign-ins | Off |
| Google sign-in | Off |
| MFA | Off (optional or required when on) |
| Signup rate limit | 30 per hour per IP |
| Sign-in rate limit | 30 per minute per IP |

## Additional resources

- [Sessions and tokens](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions) Rotation, reuse detection, and revocation.
- [External identity providers](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/external-idp) Bring your own RS256 / JWKS provider.
- [Authentication feature page](https://cubibase.com/features/authentication) The product view of CubiBase Auth.

title: Email and password
text:
# Email and password

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/email-password

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/email-password.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

POST /auth/v1/signup creates a user and returns a session. Sign in later with the password grant; the access token is the JWT for your Data API calls.

## Sign up

**Sign up · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/signup
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "mina@example.com",
  "password": "<USER_PASSWORD>"
}
```

**201 · response (trimmed)**

```json
{
  "user": {
    "id": "3f2b8c1e-9a47-4d02-b6e5-1c8f0a3d7e29",
    "email": "mina@example.com",
    "emailVerifiedAt": "2026-11-18T09:12:44.000Z",
    "providers": ["email"],
    "mfaEnabled": false
  },
  "accessToken": "<ACCESS_JWT>",
  "refreshToken": "<REFRESH_TOKEN>",
  "tokenType": "Bearer",
  "expiresIn": 3600
}
```

- The password must meet the project’s minimum length — 8 characters by default — and must not equal the email address.
- An optional `data` object is stored as the user’s metadata.
- The response carries the `user`, an `accessToken`, a `refreshToken`, and the expiry.
- A duplicate email returns `409 user_exists`.

> **note**: Email autoconfirm is on by default: the user is marked verified at signup and no confirmation email is sent. Turn autoconfirm off to manage verification yourself through the control API.

## Sign in

**Sign in · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/token?grant_type=password
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "mina@example.com",
  "password": "<USER_PASSWORD>"
}
```

A correct email and password return the same session shape as signup. Wrong credentials return `401 invalid_credentials` — the same error whether the email exists or not.

> **important**: If the user has a verified TOTP factor and MFA is on for the project, the password grant returns an MFA challenge instead of a session. See Multi-factor (TOTP).

## Using the session

1. Store the `refreshToken` safely on the client.
2. Send the `accessToken` as `Authorization: Bearer …` on Data API calls.
3. When it expires (1 hour by default), refresh with `grant_type=refresh_token` and store the new pair.
4. On sign-out, `POST /auth/v1/logout` with the refresh token revokes the session.

**Refresh · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "refreshToken": "<REFRESH_TOKEN>"
}
```

## Read and update the user

`GET /auth/v1/user` returns the signed-in user from the bearer token. `PATCH /auth/v1/user` updates the password or metadata (and converts anonymous users — see Anonymous users).

**Read the current user**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/user
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_JWT>
```

## Additional resources

- [Sessions and tokens](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions) What rotation and reuse detection mean for your client.
- [Multi-factor (TOTP)](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/mfa) The challenge flow after password sign-in.
- [Data API](https://cubibase.com/docs/data-api) Where the access token goes next.

title: Sessions and tokens
text:
# Sessions and tokens

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Access tokens live for one hour; refresh tokens for 30 days and rotate on every refresh. Reusing a replaced refresh token revokes the whole family.

## The token pair

| Token | Format | Default lifetime | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `accessToken` | HS256 JWT | 1 hour | Bearer token on Data API and user endpoints |
| `refreshToken` | Opaque, stored hashed | 30 days | Exchange for a new pair; never sent to the Data API |

The access token’s claims include `sub` (the user id), `email`, `session_id`, `amr` (how the session authenticated: `pwd`, `mfa`, `oauth`, or empty for anonymous), and the expiry. Both lifetimes are configurable per project.

## The session lifecycle

**Session lifecycle, illustration.**

1. Sign in (accessToken · 1 h). Email and password return an access JWT and a refresh token.
2. Refresh (refreshToken · rotates). A new pair is issued and the old refresh token is retired.
3. Reuse detected (family revoked). A retired token presented again revokes the whole family.
4. Revoke (session_revoked). Logout or a Console revoke fails the session on the next request.

Illustration with fictional tokens. It does not query CubiBase.

## Refreshing

**Refresh · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "refreshToken": "<REFRESH_TOKEN>"
}
```

- A refresh issues a new access token and a new refresh token, and retires the old one.
- The session id stays the same across refreshes, so the Console shows one session, not dozens.
- Store the new pair atomically: the old refresh token is dead the moment the response arrives.

> **warning**: If a replaced refresh token is presented again — a replayed copy, a stolen backup — CubiBase revokes the entire token family. The user signs in again; the attacker’s copy stops working. Treat `401 invalid_refresh_token` as “sign in again”, not “retry”.

## Revocation is immediate

Every Data API request checks that the session behind the token is still live and the user is not banned. Revoking a session (logout, or the Console’s Sessions screen) or banning a user takes effect on the next request — not when the access token expires.

**Logout · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/logout
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "refreshToken": "<REFRESH_TOKEN>"
}
```

| Situation | Next request returns |
| --- | --- |
| Session revoked | `401 session_revoked` |
| User banned | `403 user_banned` |
| Project requires MFA, session lacks it | `401 mfa_required` |
| Access token expired | `401 invalid_token` |

## Additional resources

- [Email and password](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/email-password) Where the first pair comes from.
- [Multi-factor (TOTP)](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/mfa) Sessions that carry an MFA verification.

title: Anonymous users
text:
# Anonymous users

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/anonymous

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/anonymous.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Let visitors use your app before they create an account. An anonymous user is a real user with a real id — and converting them later keeps every row they wrote, with a password or with Google (no password needed).

## Enable anonymous sign-ins

1. **Open the provider settings** — Console → your project → Auth → Providers → Anonymous users.
2. **Switch on Allow anonymous sign-ins** — The setting is off by default. Turning it off later blocks new anonymous sessions but does not touch existing ones.

> **note**: Anonymous sign-ins follow the project signup switch and the signup rate limit, and anonymous users count toward the plan’s end-user quota.

## Sign a visitor in

`POST /auth/v1/signup/anonymous` needs no email or password. CubiBase creates a real user in `auth.users` with `is_anonymous` set and returns the same session shape as a normal signup.

**Anonymous sign-in · request**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/signup/anonymous
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "data": { "cart": ["item-1"] }
}
```

**201 · response (trimmed)**

```json
{
  "user": {
    "id": "3f2b8c1e-9a47-4d02-b6e5-1c8f0a3d7e29",
    "email": null,
    "isAnonymous": true,
    "providers": [],
    "mfaEnabled": false
  },
  "accessToken": "<ACCESS_JWT>",
  "refreshToken": "<REFRESH_TOKEN>",
  "tokenType": "Bearer",
  "expiresIn": 3600
}
```

The access token works like any other end-user JWT: its `sub` is the user id, so rows written with a user column already belong to that visitor.

## Convert to a real account

An anonymous visitor becomes a real account in place — same user id, same rows. There are two ways to do it, and Google never asks for a password:

| Path | What the visitor does | What you send |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Email + password | Types an email and chooses a password | `PATCH /auth/v1/user` with the anonymous bearer token, `email`, and `password` |
| Google | Clicks “Continue with Google” — Google proves who they are | The anonymous bearer token on `/auth/v1/authorize` or `grant_type=id_token` |

> **important**: With Google, the Google account is the credential: CubiBase sets the email from the verified Google profile and clears `is_anonymous` — no password is created or required. The visitor signs in with Google from then on.

- The user id does not change on either path — the rows they created stay theirs.
- Existing sessions keep working; no re-login is forced.
- Metadata is merged with the Google profile (name, picture).

## Path 1 · email and password

When the visitor is ready to register with an email, convert the account with `PATCH /auth/v1/user`, sending the anonymous bearer token plus an email and a password.

**Convert · same user id**

```http
PATCH https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/user
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "email": "mina@example.com",
  "password": "<USER_PASSWORD>"
}
```

> **important**: On this endpoint conversion requires both email and password in one request (`400 conversion_requires_credentials` otherwise). A duplicate email returns `409 user_exists`. If the visitor prefers Google, use Path 2 instead — no password needed.

## Path 2 · Google (no password)

The trick is one header: send the anonymous user’s access token as `Authorization: Bearer …` on the Google sign-in request. CubiBase then links the Google identity to that user instead of creating a new one. Both Google flows support it.

### Browser redirect flow

1. **Start the flow with the anonymous bearer token** — Call GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=google&redirect_to=… with the apikey header and the anonymous access token as the bearer. CubiBase remembers the user id inside the single-use state.
2. **The visitor consents at Google** — Open the returned url in the browser. Google shows its consent screen — no CubiBase password is involved at any point.
3. **The callback converts the account** — Google redirects back to CubiBase, which links the identity to the remembered user: the email comes from the Google profile, is_anonymous is cleared, and the user id stays the same.
4. **Store the new session** — The browser lands on your redirect_to with a fresh token pair in the URL fragment (amr: ["oauth"]). Replace the anonymous pair with it; the old anonymous session keeps working until it expires or is revoked.

**Authorize · with the anonymous bearer token**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/authorize?provider=google&redirect_to=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fauth%2Fcallback
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_JWT>
```

### ID-token flow (mobile and web SDKs)

If your app already holds a Google ID token from Google Sign-In, post it to the id_token grant with the same anonymous bearer token. The response is a normal session for the converted user.

**Link a Google ID token · same user id**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/token?grant_type=id_token
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <ANONYMOUS_ACCESS_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "google",
  "idToken": "<GOOGLE_ID_TOKEN>"
}
```

> **warning**: Without the anonymous bearer token, Google sign-in creates a brand-new user — the visitor’s anonymous rows stay behind on the old id. Always send the header while the visitor is still anonymous.

> **note**: Because an anonymous user has no email yet, any Google account can be linked. A Google account already linked to another user returns `409 identity_exists`. The email-match rule (`409 email_mismatch`) only applies to users who already have an email.

## Managing anonymous users

In the Console user directory, anonymous users carry an Anonymous badge and can be filtered separately. From the SQL editor you can inspect them directly:

**SQL · count anonymous users**

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS anonymous_users
FROM auth.users
WHERE is_anonymous;
```

## Additional resources

- [Google sign-in](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/google) Both Google flows in depth — the bearer-token header is what converts an anonymous user.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) Why anonymous rows are already protected.
- [Quotas](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/quotas) Anonymous users count toward the end-user limit.

title: Google sign-in
text:
# Google sign-in

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/google

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/google.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Create an OAuth client in the Google Cloud Console, paste its credentials into CubiBase, and register the callback URL. Two flows: browser redirect, or a Google ID token your app already holds.

## Configure it step by step

Everything happens in two places: console.cloud.google.com for the Google side, and Console → project → Auth → Providers → Google for the CubiBase side.

1. **Google: select or create a project** — Open console.cloud.google.com and pick the Google Cloud project for your app.
2. **Google: configure the OAuth consent screen** — APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen. Choose External, fill in the app name and the support and developer contact emails, and add the scopes openid, email, and profile. While the app is in Testing, only listed test users can sign in; publish to production when you are ready for everyone.
3. **Google: create an OAuth client** — APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID → Web application.
4. **Google: register the redirect URI** — Copy the Authorized redirect URI that the CubiBase Google section displays — it looks like https://{slug}.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/callback?provider=google&project={projectId}. Paste it exactly, query parameters included.
5. **CubiBase: enable the provider** — In Auth → Providers → Google, tick Enable Google sign-in, paste the Client ID and Client secret, and save. The secret is stored encrypted and never shown again; the section shows a Secret stored badge instead.
6. **CubiBase: allowlist your app’s URLs** — In the same form, fill the App redirect allowlist with the URLs in your app that should receive the session — one per line; a trailing * allows prefix matches. Loopback HTTP redirect URLs are always allowed for native and local development.

> **warning**: The redirect URI must match character for character, including the `provider` and `project` query parameters. A mismatch is the most common cause of Google’s “redirect_uri_mismatch” error.

## The browser redirect flow

**Google sign-in redirect flow, illustration.** Your app asks for a consent url → GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=google → CubiBase Auth (single-use state) → browser opens Google consent → Google (user consents) → redirect to /auth/v1/callback → CubiBase callback (verifies code + state) → 302 · your redirect_to with #access_token=… refresh_token=… expires_in=3600.

Illustration. The session rides in the URL fragment, which browsers never send to servers.

Your app starts the flow with `GET /auth/v1/authorize?provider=google&redirect_to={your callback URL}`, sending the publishable key. The response contains a `url`: send the browser there.

**1 · Start the flow**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/authorize?provider=google&redirect_to=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fauth%2Fcallback
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
```

**2 · Response: open this url**

```json
{
  "url": "https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?client_id=…&redirect_uri=…&response_type=code&scope=openid%20email%20profile&state=…",
  "state": "<SINGLE_USE_STATE>",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-20T10:10:00.000Z"
}
```

Google shows its consent screen and redirects back to the CubiBase callback, which verifies the response and redirects the browser to your `redirect_to` with the session in the URL fragment (the part after `#`).

**3 · Your callback page reads the fragment**

```text
https://app.example.com/auth/callback#access_token=<ACCESS_JWT>&refresh_token=<REFRESH_TOKEN>&token_type=Bearer&expires_in=3600&expires_at=2026-11-20T11%3A00%3A00.000Z
```

> **tip**: Read the tokens from `location.hash` on your callback page and store them like any CubiBase session. Fragments are never sent to servers or access logs. If the user denies consent or something fails, the same redirect carries an `error` query parameter instead.

## The ID-token flow (mobile and web SDKs)

If your app already obtains a Google ID token — Google Sign-In on Android, iOS, or the web — skip the redirect flow and POST it to `/auth/v1/token?grant_type=id_token` with the publishable key.

**Verify a Google ID token**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/token?grant_type=id_token
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "provider": "google",
  "idToken": "<GOOGLE_ID_TOKEN>"
}
```

CubiBase verifies the token’s RS256 signature against Google’s published keys, the issuer, the audience (your Client ID), and the expiry, then returns a normal session. Pass a `nonce` to bind the token to your sign-in attempt.

## Identity rules (both flows)

| Situation | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Google account has signed in before | Signs straight in |
| Request carries an end-user bearer token | The Google identity links to that user — the anonymous upgrade path |
| Verified Google email matches an existing user | The identity attaches to that account |
| New Google account | Signs up a new user (the signup switch applies) |
| User has a verified factor, project requires MFA | `403 mfa_required` — Google alone does not satisfy MFA |

> **tip**: Converting an anonymous visitor? Send their access token as `Authorization: Bearer …` on the authorize request (or on the id_token grant). The Google identity then links to that same user — no password involved. Step by step in Anonymous users → Path 2.

> **note**: Linking checks the email: a Google account whose email differs from the signed-in user’s email is refused with `409 email_mismatch`. Anonymous users have no email yet, so any Google account links and converts them. A Google account already linked to another user returns `409 identity_exists`.

## Additional resources

- [Anonymous users](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/anonymous) The conversion path Google linking completes.
- [Sessions and tokens](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions) The session both flows return.
- [Multi-factor (TOTP)](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/mfa) Why Google sign-in still asks for a code sometimes.

title: Multi-factor authentication (TOTP)
text:
# Multi-factor authentication (TOTP)

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/mfa

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/mfa.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Users enroll an authenticator app; sign-in then returns a challenge that a six-digit code completes. MFA can be optional per user or required for the whole project.

## Enable MFA for the project

1. **Open the MFA settings** — Console → your project → Auth → Multi-factor.
2. **Enable MFA** — Users can now enroll a TOTP authenticator. Optionally make MFA required: every session must then include a verified factor.

## Enroll an authenticator

`POST /auth/v1/factors` with the bearer token returns a TOTP secret and an `otpauth://` URI. Render the URI as a QR code (or show the secret for manual entry), then confirm the first code with `POST /auth/v1/factors/verify`.

**1 · Enroll · response**

```json
{
  "factorId": "b2e6f0a4-7c19-4d83-9e51-6a0c2d8b4f37",
  "secret": "<TOTP_SECRET>",
  "uri": "otpauth://totp/CubiBase%20example-project:mina%40example.com?secret=…&issuer=…"
}
```

**2 · Verify the first code**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/factors/verify
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_JWT>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "factorId": "b2e6f0a4-7c19-4d83-9e51-6a0c2d8b4f37",
  "code": "123456"
}
```

> **note**: A factor only counts after the first code verifies. Remove a factor with `DELETE /auth/v1/factors/{factorId}`; the Console can also remove factors for a user.

## Sign-in with a challenge

When a user with a verified factor signs in with a password, the token grant returns an MFA challenge instead of a session:

**Password grant · MFA challenge**

```json
{
  "mfaRequired": true,
  "challengeId": "9d41c7a2-5b18-4e6f-a0d3-2e7b9c4f1a58",
  "factorId": "b2e6f0a4-7c19-4d83-9e51-6a0c2d8b4f37",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-18T09:17:44.000Z"
}
```

Post the challenge id and the current code to complete the sign-in. Challenges expire after five minutes and are single-use.

**Complete the challenge**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/auth/v1/token?grant_type=mfa
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "challengeId": "9d41c7a2-5b18-4e6f-a0d3-2e7b9c4f1a58",
  "code": "123456"
}
```

The response is a normal session whose tokens carry `amr: ["pwd", "mfa"]` — the proof Data API requests check when the project requires MFA.

## Required MFA

- Every session must include a verified factor; sessions without it fail Data API calls with `401 mfa_required`.
- A user without a factor cannot sign in until they enroll: the password grant returns `403 mfa_enrollment_required`.
- Google sign-in does not replace MFA for users with a verified factor — they must use password + TOTP.
- Code attempts are rate-limited (10 per minute per IP by default).

## Additional resources

- [Sessions and tokens](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/sessions) How the amr claim travels with the session.
- [Email and password](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/email-password) The grant that starts the challenge.

title: External identity providers
text:
# External identity providers

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/external-idp

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth/external-idp.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

If your users already sign in elsewhere, keep that provider. Configure a JWKS URL, issuer, and audience, and CubiBase verifies its RS256 tokens on every request.

## Configure the provider

| Setting | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| JWKS URL | Where CubiBase fetches the provider’s public signing keys (HTTPS, cached 5 minutes) |
| Issuer (`iss`) | Must match the token’s issuer claim |
| Audience (`aud`) | Must match the token’s audience claim |
| Allowed algorithms | The token’s `alg` must be allowed for the project |

On every Data API request, CubiBase verifies the RS256 signature against the JWKS, checks issuer, audience, and expiry, and uses the verified `sub` as the user id for the transaction — so user-column policies work with your own ids.

> **important**: CubiBase Auth and an external provider are alternatives: a project’s requests are checked against the provider configuration you set. Google is the built-in social provider; other social buttons and SAML are not part of the current engine.

## Development tokens

While building, a development endpoint can issue an HS256 token for a user id you choose, when that issuer is enabled for the project. Use it to seed data and test policies before your real sign-in is wired up.

> **warning**: Development tokens are for building, not production traffic. Switch the project to your real provider (or CubiBase Auth) before you ship.

## Plan availability

Bring-your-own-IdP (RS256 / JWKS) is available on the Pro and Business plans. The Free plan uses CubiBase Auth.

## Additional resources

- [Authentication overview](https://cubibase.com/docs/auth) The built-in alternative: CubiBase Auth.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) How the verified sub becomes row access.
- [Plans](https://cubibase.com/pricing) Where external IdP support sits.

title: API keys
text:
# API keys

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/api-keys

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/api-keys.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

The publishable key identifies your project to the API. It is meant to live in your client — but it never authorizes rows by itself.

## Two kinds of key

| Key | Prefix | Where it lives | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Publishable | `cb_pub_` | Your app (browser, mobile) | Identifies the project on every Data API and Auth call |
| Secret | `cb_sec_` | Server-side only (trusted servers, AI agents) | Authenticates Data API and RPC calls as the service actor; shown once, stored hashed |

> **important**: Never ship a secret key in a browser or mobile client. It acts with service-level access to every row a service policy grants. Keep it on your server or in an agent environment.

## Using the secret key (service actor)

A secret key authenticates REST and RPC calls without an end-user JWT. Send it as the `apikey` header or as `Authorization: Bearer`. The request runs with `cubibase.role = 'service'` and an empty `cubibase.user_id()`. Row-level security still applies — a table without a service policy returns no rows.

**Service request**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers
apikey: cb_sec_…
```

Grant service access explicitly with a policy, for example `cubibase.current_role() = 'service'` for SELECT, or keep service access limited to SECURITY DEFINER functions. Every service write is recorded in the audit log.

## Using the publishable key

Send it in the `apikey` header on every request to the project host — Data API and Auth alike. The engine checks it against the project resolved from the host.

**Every request carries both headers**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/rest/v1/customers
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT>
```

| Situation | Response |
| --- | --- |
| No `apikey` header | `401 missing_api_key` |
| Key not valid for this project | `401 invalid_api_key` |
| Valid key, no bearer token and no secret key | `401 missing_end_user_token` |

## Keeping keys safe

- The publishable key is public by design, but treat it as a project credential: it names your project to the API.
- Row access comes from the end-user JWT and the table’s policies — not from the key.
- Manage keys from Console → project → API keys: create, revoke, and rotate.
- If a key leaks and you want it dead, revoke it; requests using it fail immediately.

## Additional resources

- [How CubiBase works](https://cubibase.com/docs/architecture) Where the key check sits in the request path.
- [Row-level security](https://cubibase.com/docs/database/row-level-security) What actually authorizes rows.

title: Personal access tokens
text:
# Personal access tokens

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/access-tokens

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/access-tokens.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Personal access tokens (cb_pat_…) authenticate the Control API without an interactive login — for scripts, CI, and AI agents. Create them in Console → Account → Access tokens.

## What a token is

A personal access token (PAT) is a developer credential for the Control API at api.cubibase.com. It carries the permissions of the account that created it, narrowed by a scope and an optional project restriction. Tokens are shown once at creation and stored only as SHA-256 hashes.

| Scope | Allows |
| --- | --- |
| read | GET routes: list projects, schema, rows, logs, usage |
| write | Everything in read, plus creating and modifying projects, tables, policies, keys |
| admin | Everything in write, plus destructive operations such as project deletion |

Scopes are cumulative: write includes read, admin includes write. A token can also be restricted to a single project, and can carry an expiration date.

## Creating and using a token

1. **Open the Console** — Account → Access tokens → Create token. Pick a name, scope, optional project restriction and expiry.
2. **Copy the token** — The cb_pat_… value is shown exactly once. Store it in a secret manager or environment variable.
3. **Call the Control API** — Send Authorization: Bearer cb_pat_… on any api.cubibase.com route within the token’s scope.

**List projects with a PAT**

```bash
curl https://api.cubibase.com/v1/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer cb_pat_…"
```

> **note**: Tokens cannot manage other tokens: the /v1/auth/tokens routes require an interactive session. This prevents a leaked token from minting new credentials.

## Rate limits and revocation

- Token requests are rate-limited per token. A throttled request returns 429 with a Retry-After header — wait that many seconds and retry.
- Revoke a token from the same Console page; requests using it fail immediately with 401.
- Every token records a last-used timestamp so you can find and revoke stale credentials.
- Errors always carry a stable machine code and a requestId, e.g. {"error":{"code":"insufficient_scope","message":"…","requestId":"…"}}.

## Additional resources

- [Using CubiBase with AI agents](https://cubibase.com/docs/agents) MCP server, CLI, and the agent workflow built on these tokens.
- [API keys](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/api-keys) The project-level keys for the Data API.

title: Quotas and suspension
text:
# Quotas and suspension

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/quotas

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/quotas.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Each plan sets project slots, an independent database quota per project, and consumption quotas shared across your organization. Hitting a limit refuses new growth — reads keep working, and data is never deleted for exceeding a quota.

## What the plans limit

| Quota | Scope | Measured as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project slots | Organization | Every plan includes one project; paid plans add purchased additional-project slots. Paused projects still count |
| Database size | Per project | The project database’s size on disk, independent for every project |
| Monthly active users | Organization (shared) | Unique end users who authenticated this cycle, across all projects |
| API requests per month | Organization (shared) | Data API requests across all projects |
| Total bandwidth per month | Organization (shared) | Outbound bytes delivered to customers this cycle — API responses plus file delivery, combined |
| API bandwidth sublimit per month | Organization (shared) | API response bytes this cycle; a sublimit of total bandwidth, not an extra allowance |
| Object storage | Organization (shared) | Ready objects across all projects, plus bytes reserved by in-flight uploads |
| Storage write operations | Organization (shared) | Completed uploads and server-side writes this cycle |
| File download requests | Organization (shared) | Authorized downloads this cycle |
| CloudFront requests | Organization (shared) | Combined API and file-delivery edge requests this cycle |
| Function invocations and compute | Organization (shared) | Executed runs and GB-seconds this cycle |
| Maximum file size | Technical (per operation) | The smaller of the plan maximum and the bucket’s own cap |

Database storage is allocated per project; all other consumption quotas are shared across the organization. Buying additional projects adds project slots and per-project database storage — it never increases the shared quotas. Total bandwidth covers API responses and file delivery together; the API bandwidth sublimit never blocks your remaining file bandwidth. The numbers for each plan are on the pricing page. The Console’s Usage page shows consumption against every limit, with warnings at 50%, 75%, 90% and 100%.

> **Optional additional usage (V4.5)**: By default every limit below is a hard stop. Pro and Business organizations can explicitly enable additional usage in Console → Billing → Additional Usage: consumption beyond the included quotas is then billed at published per-unit rates under a monthly spending limit the organization sets, instead of being refused. Free plans are never eligible, nothing is enabled automatically, and reaching the spending limit returns 402 spending_limit_reached while included quotas, billing access and deletion keep working. Rates and rules are on the pricing page.

## When a project hits a limit

| Limit reached | What is refused | What keeps working |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project slots | Creating another project (`402 quota_exceeded`). Free: upgrade to Pro required. Paid: purchase additional project slots | All existing projects keep working |
| Monthly active users | New signups and first-time activations (`402 quota_exceeded`) | Sign-ins, reads, writes by existing active users |
| Database size | New writes (`402 quota_exceeded`) | All reads |
| Object storage | New uploads (`402 STORAGE_ACCOUNT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED`) | Downloads within bandwidth, deletions, upgrades |
| Total bandwidth (API + file delivery) | Further downloads and API responses once the combined allowance is exhausted (`402 quota_exceeded`) | Metadata, listings, uploads; resets next billing cycle |
| API bandwidth sublimit | Further API responses (`402 quota_exceeded`) | File downloads against remaining total bandwidth keep working |

> **note**: Nothing is deleted when a quota is reached. Remove data or users you no longer need, or upgrade the plan, and the refused operations resume.

## Account suspension

If the whole account stays over its plan limits — too many projects, an oversized database, or too many end users — we email a warning and start a 7-day grace period. Organizations with additional usage enabled and spending headroom are not suspended for billed excess (database storage, end users); the excess is metered under their spending limit instead. Project-slot limits always apply: additional projects are a fixed subscription item, never metered usage.

1. **Warning email** — The account is over its limits. The 7-day grace period starts.
2. **Still over after 7 days** — All of the account’s projects are suspended: the Data API, auth, and Console tools stop serving them and return 403 project_suspended.
3. **Back within limits** — Suspension ends automatically. Upgrade to Pro or Business, or delete projects, data, or users — suspended projects reactivate on their own.

> **important**: Data is never deleted for exceeding a quota. Upgrading applies the higher limits to the same projects and databases — nothing is migrated.

## Changing plans

Upgrades and downgrades are self-serve in the Console and prorated by Stripe. Switching between Pro and Business changes only the base plan: every purchased project slot and its monthly add-on charge stays exactly as it is. Before any change is confirmed, the Console shows a consolidated preview: the new monthly total, your unchanged purchased project slots, and — for downgrades — whether your current usage fits the smaller plan.

1. **Upgrades** — Apply immediately with prorations. Switching between Pro and Business preserves your purchased project slots, their quantity and their charges — only the base plan price changes.
2. **Downgrade validation** — CubiBase checks your project count (paused projects count), each project’s database size against the target per-project quota, and your shared object storage. If anything does not fit, the change is refused with a list of exactly what to resolve.
3. **Resolve, then confirm** — Delete projects or objects you no longer need. Purchased project slots stay purchased across paid plan changes; reducing them is a separate, explicit action scheduled for the next renewal. A scheduled slot reduction must be cancelled before a plan change. Nothing is ever deleted automatically to make a downgrade fit.
4. **Monthly consumption** — If this cycle’s consumption already exceeds a smaller allowance, that resource is blocked after the downgrade until the next cycle reset — reads keep working and no data is deleted.

> **note**: Returning to Free happens by cancelling the subscription in the Stripe billing portal; the plan stays active until the period end. The same usage checks apply before the Free limits take effect.

## Additional resources

- [Plans and limits](https://cubibase.com/pricing) The numbers per plan.
- [Pause, archive, restore](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/lifecycle) The separate inactivity policy for Free projects.

title: Pause, archive, restore
text:
# Pause, archive, restore

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/lifecycle

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/lifecycle.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Free projects must stay in use. After 14 idle days a project is paused; after 60 paused days it is archived to a downloadable backup. Nothing is ever lost.

## The inactivity timeline

**Free-plan inactivity timeline.**

1. Active (serving traffic). API, auth, and Console work normally. Any request or Console visit counts as activity.
2. Paused (after 14 idle days). Free projects only. Requests return 403 project_paused; the database is untouched. Resume is instant.
3. Archived (after 60 paused days). A full .backup file is stored and the live database is removed. The backup is kept, never auto-deleted.
4. Restored (Resume anytime). CubiBase recreates the database and restores the backup: tables, rows, users, and policies included.

Illustration of the Free-plan inactivity timeline. Paid plans are never paused for inactivity.

Activity means a Data API or auth request, or opening the project in the Console. Paid plans (Pro and Business) are never paused for inactivity.

## Paused (day 14)

- The API and auth return `403 project_paused`; the owner is emailed.
- The database is left intact — nothing is archived yet.
- Resume from the Console project page with one click. While the database exists, the resume is instant.
- Reminder emails arrive around day 30, day 45, and one week before the deadline.

## Archived (day 60 of being paused)

- CubiBase takes a full PostgreSQL backup (`pg_dump` custom format, a `.backup` file) and stores it.
- The live database is removed to stop storage costs.
- The backup is kept — it is not auto-deleted — and the project’s API keys and configuration survive.

> **note**: An archived project is not lost. Download the `.backup` file from the Console project page at any time, or click Resume to bring the project back.

## Restoring

Resume on an archived project recreates the database and restores the backup automatically — tables, rows, users, and row-level security policies included. The project is active again with the same slug, host, and keys.

You can also restore the `.backup` on your own PostgreSQL server:

**Restore on your own server**

```text
pg_restore -d my_database example-project.backup
```

## Additional resources

- [Quotas and suspension](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/quotas) The other reason a project can stop serving.
- [Plans](https://cubibase.com/pricing) Paid plans are never paused for inactivity.

title: Storage overview
text:
# Storage overview

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/storage

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

S3-backed object storage on your project host at /storage/v1. Public and private buckets, direct browser uploads, metered downloads, and server-enforced quotas.

## How Storage is organized

Each project has buckets, and each bucket holds objects at logical paths such as `images/avatar.png`. Folders are path prefixes only — nothing is created for them. The catalog (buckets, objects, upload sessions, events) lives in a managed `storage` schema in your project’s PostgreSQL database. The file bytes live in the deployment’s private, encrypted S3 bucket under opaque platform-generated keys; your filenames never become S3 keys.

| Piece | Where it lives | Who can touch it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bucket and object metadata | Project database, `storage` schema | The engine only — not the Data API or SQL roles’ writes |
| File bytes | Private S3 bucket, encrypted at rest | The engine’s IAM role; clients via short-lived authorizations |
| Quota accounting | Central metadata database | The engine, atomically per upload and download |

## Authentication

Storage reuses the platform credentials. Every request carries the `apikey` header with the project’s publishable key. Writes and private reads additionally need an `Authorization: Bearer` token: either an end-user JWT from CubiBase Auth, or a secret API key (`cb_sec_…`) for trusted server code. Public-bucket reads need only the publishable key.

| Credential | Can do |
| --- | --- |
| Publishable key alone | Read objects in public buckets (metered) |
| Publishable key + user JWT | Upload, list, read, and delete according to bucket visibility and object ownership |
| Publishable key + secret API key | Full project-scoped access — still subject to every quota |
| Signed download token | Read exactly one object until the token expires |

> **important**: Secret API keys are server-side credentials. Never ship them in a browser or mobile bundle. Quotas, project isolation, and audit logging apply to them exactly like to any other caller.

## Route map

| Call | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /storage/v1/buckets` | Create a bucket |
| `GET /storage/v1/buckets` | List buckets |
| `GET /storage/v1/buckets/{bucket}` | Bucket configuration |
| `PATCH /storage/v1/buckets/{bucket}` | Update visibility, size cap, MIME allowlist |
| `DELETE /storage/v1/buckets/{bucket}` | Delete the bucket and its objects |
| `POST /storage/v1/objects/upload` | Start an upload (reserves quota, returns the S3 policy) |
| `POST /storage/v1/uploads/{id}/complete` | Verify and finalize the uploaded object |
| `GET /storage/v1/uploads/{id}` | Upload session status |
| `GET /storage/v1/objects` | List objects by bucket, prefix, and search |
| `GET /storage/v1/objects/{id}` | Object metadata |
| `GET /storage/v1/objects/{id}/content` | Download (metered; Range supported) |
| `POST /storage/v1/objects/{id}/sign` | Short-lived signed download link |
| `GET /storage/v1/public/{bucket}/{path}` | Anonymous public-bucket read (metered) |
| `DELETE /storage/v1/objects/{id}` | Delete an object |
| `GET /storage/v1/usage` | This project’s storage and bandwidth consumption |

**List objects · prefix browsing**

```http
GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/objects?bucket=avatars&prefix=images/&delimiter=true&limit=50
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT_OR_SECRET_KEY>
```

## In the Console

Open a project and choose Storage. The overview shows project, account, and bandwidth quotas with warnings at 50%, 75%, 90%, and 100%. Buckets manages visibility and limits; Files is a prefix-based browser with drag-and-drop uploads, downloads, share links, and deletion. Console traffic passes through the same quota and event machinery as the API — there is no unmetered side door.

- [Buckets](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/buckets) Create and configure public and private buckets.
- [Uploading files](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/uploads) The three-step direct-to-S3 upload contract.
- [Downloads and sharing](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/downloads) Public URLs, authorized reads, and signed links.
- [Quotas and errors](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/quotas) Limits per plan and the machine-readable error codes.

## Additional resources

- [Storage security](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/security) Isolation, path safety, and what public really means.
- [Object events](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/events) The durable event contract and function triggers.
- [Storage feature page](https://cubibase.com/features/storage) The product-level overview.

title: Buckets
text:
# Buckets

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/buckets

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/buckets.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

A bucket is a named container with a visibility mode, an optional file size cap, and an optional MIME allowlist. Names are unique within the project.

## Create a bucket

Bucket names are 2–63 characters: lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes, and underscores, starting with a letter or digit. Creating, updating, and deleting buckets requires a secret API key (or a Console owner/admin session).

**POST /storage/v1/buckets**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/buckets
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <SECRET_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "avatars",
  "public": true,
  "allowedMimeTypes": ["image/*"]
}
```

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string, required | Unique within the project |
| `public` | boolean, default `false` | `true` = anonymous read-only downloads |
| `fileSizeLimitBytes` | integer or null | Per-bucket cap; can only lower the plan maximum |
| `allowedMimeTypes` | string[] or null | Allowlist of exact types or `type/*` wildcards; null allows any |

## Public versus private

- Public: anyone with the publishable key can read published objects at `/storage/v1/public/{bucket}/{path}`. Reads are metered against bandwidth.
- Private: reads require an end-user JWT, a secret API key, or a signed download token. Listing private metadata always requires authorization.
- Neither mode allows anonymous uploads, overwrites, or deletions. Public is a read setting, not a write setting.
- Visibility can be flipped at any time with `PATCH`; existing signed links keep their expiry.

## Size cap and MIME allowlist

The effective maximum file size is the smaller of the plan limit and the bucket cap. The MIME allowlist is checked twice: against the declared type when the upload starts, and against the verified content type reported by S3 at completion — a client cannot sneak a disallowed type past it by lying in the request.

> **note**: Deleting a bucket deletes every object inside it from S3 and the catalog, and returns the bytes to your quota. The Console asks for confirmation; the API does not.

## Additional resources

- [Uploading files](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/uploads) Start an upload into your new bucket.
- [Quotas and errors](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/quotas) How the plan and bucket caps interact.

title: Uploading files
text:
# Uploading files

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/uploads

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/uploads.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Uploads go directly from the client to S3. The engine reserves quota first, issues a short-lived policy pinned to one staging key and the exact size, then verifies and finalizes the object.

## The three-step contract

1. **Start the upload** — POST the bucket, logical path, exact size in bytes, and MIME type. The engine validates the path, checks the plan and bucket limits, and atomically reserves the bytes against both the project and the account quota. If any limit would be exceeded, the request fails before any authorization is issued.
2. **POST the file to S3** — Build a multipart form: every field from the response’s upload.fields first, then Content-Type, then the file part last. POST it to upload.url. The policy pins the exact staging key and a content-length-range equal to the declared size, so S3 itself rejects any other size or destination.
3. **Complete the session** — POST to /storage/v1/uploads/{id}/complete. The engine heads the staged object, verifies its exact size and MIME type, copies it to its final key, converts the reservation into committed usage, and records the creation event — all in one transaction. Completion is idempotent: calling it twice returns the same object.

**1 · Start the upload**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/objects/upload
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT_OR_SECRET_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "bucket": "avatars",
  "path": "images/mika.png",
  "sizeBytes": 182344,
  "mimeType": "image/png",
  "overwrite": false
}
```

**Response (trimmed)**

```json
{
  "uploadId": "f2c6…",
  "objectId": "9b1e…",
  "bucket": "avatars",
  "path": "images/mika.png",
  "upload": {
    "url": "https://<deployment-bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com",
    "fields": { "key": "staging/<project>/<upload>", "policy": "…", "x-amz-signature": "…" },
    "method": "POST"
  },
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-20T10:10:00.000Z"
}
```

**3 · Complete**

```http
POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/uploads/<UPLOAD_ID>/complete
apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY
Authorization: Bearer <USER_JWT_OR_SECRET_KEY>
```

## Browser example

**JavaScript · fetch + FormData**

```ts
const start = await fetch(`https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/objects/upload`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    apikey: PUBLISHABLE_KEY,
    authorization: `Bearer ${userJwt}`,
    'content-type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    bucket: 'avatars',
    path: `images/${file.name}`,
    sizeBytes: file.size,
    mimeType: file.type,
    overwrite: false,
  }),
}).then((r) => r.json());

const form = new FormData();
for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(start.upload.fields)) form.append(k, v);
form.append('Content-Type', file.type);
form.append('file', file); // must be the last part
await fetch(start.upload.url, { method: 'POST', body: form });

await fetch(`https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/uploads/${start.uploadId}/complete`, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { apikey: PUBLISHABLE_KEY, authorization: `Bearer ${userJwt}` },
});
```

## Overwrites and expiry

- A path that already holds a ready object rejects the upload with `409 storage_object_exists` unless you pass `overwrite: true`.
- Overwrite accounting uses the net change: replacing a 1 MB file with a 2 MB file commits +1 MB, not +2 MB.
- Sessions expire (default 5 minutes). An expired session releases its reservation and can never be completed; start a new upload.
- Failed or abandoned uploads never produce a downloadable object and never emit a creation event. Staging keys are cleaned up by a lifecycle rule and a cleanup worker.

> **warning**: The declared size must equal the actual file size exactly. S3 enforces the content-length-range, and completion re-verifies the size — a mismatch fails the session and releases the reservation.

## Additional resources

- [Downloads and sharing](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/downloads) Read the file back.
- [Quotas and errors](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/quotas) What a rejected reservation looks like.

title: Downloads and sharing
text: # Downloads and sharing Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/downloads Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/downloads.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt) Every download streams through the engine and is metered byte-accurately against the account’s monthly bandwidth. Public URLs, authorized reads, and signed links all use the same metered path. ## Public files Objects in public buckets are readable by logical path with only the publishable key. The route is stable and safe to embed in `` tags or share. Private buckets return `404` on this route — they look absent, not forbidden. **Public read** ```http GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/public/avatars/images/mika.png apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY ``` ## Private files Read private objects by id with an end-user JWT or a secret API key. `GET /storage/v1/objects/{id}` returns metadata only; the bytes come from `/content`. **Authorized read** ```http GET https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/objects//content apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY Authorization: Bearer ``` ## Signed download links To share a private file without sharing credentials, sign it. The token is scoped to exactly one object, expires after a short deployment-configured lifetime (5 minutes by default), and cannot open any other object. Anyone with the link can read that one file until expiry — and the download counts against bandwidth like any other. **Sign an object** ```http POST https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/objects//sign apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json {} ``` The response’s `url` is the download URL with the token attached: `/storage/v1/objects/{id}/content?token=…`. Expired or tampered tokens are rejected with `401`. ## Ranges, cancellation, and metering - `Range: bytes=start-end` is supported and returns `206` with a truthful `Content-Range`. Only the requested bytes are billed. - A canceled download is billed only for the bytes actually delivered; the rest of the reservation is refunded. - If the remaining monthly budget is smaller than the file, the engine delivers a partial `206` response capped at the budget, then refuses further downloads with `402`. - There are no presigned S3 GET URLs anywhere in the platform: every billable byte passes the meter. > **note**: Engine-proxied delivery is the current design so quota enforcement is real-time. A CDN/edge delivery path that preserves the same accounting is planned future work. ## Deleting objects Deletion requires write authorization. The engine removes the bytes from S3 first and only then decrements usage and records the deletion event — usage never drops for a file that still exists. **Delete** ```http DELETE https://example-project.api.cubibase.com/storage/v1/objects/ apikey: cb_pub_EXAMPLE_ONLY Authorization: Bearer ``` ## Additional resources - [Quotas and errors](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/quotas) Bandwidth limits and reset behavior. - [Storage security](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/security) Token scoping and isolation.

# Storage quotas and errors

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/quotas

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/quotas.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Every storage limit is enforced on the server before the operation happens. By default quotas are hard stops, never automatic charges, and reaching one never deletes a file. Paid plans can opt in to metered additional usage with a spending limit.

## Limits per plan

| Quota | Free | Pro | Business |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Object storage (organization, shared) | 2 GB | 100 GB | 250 GB |
| Monthly total bandwidth (organization; API + file delivery) | 15 GB | 500 GB | 750 GB |
| Monthly API bandwidth sublimit (organization) | 5 GB | 25 GB | 100 GB |
| Monthly file download requests (organization) | 100,000 | 250,000 | 2,000,000 |
| Monthly storage write operations (organization) | 10,000 | 100,000 | 300,000 |
| Maximum file size | 50 MB | 1 GB | 5 GB |

Sizes use binary units: 1 GB = 1024 MB = 1,073,741,824 bytes. Object storage is one shared organization capacity across all projects; it is checked atomically when an upload reserves bytes, so concurrent uploads cannot race past it. Bandwidth, download requests and write operations reset with the organization’s billing cycle. Buying additional projects does not increase these shared quotas.

## Behavior at the limits

| Limit reached | Blocked | Still available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organization storage | New uploads | Downloads (within bandwidth), deletions, upgrades |
| Monthly bandwidth | Further downloads | Metadata, listings, uploads, deletions |
| Maximum file size | That upload | Smaller files |
| Downgrade below usage | New uploads until usage fits | All existing files, downloads within the new bandwidth |

> **note**: Deleting objects frees capacity immediately. Upgrading raises the limits on the same project — nothing is migrated or deleted.

## Error codes

Quota and access failures return the platform error envelope with a stable machine-readable code and details describing the limit and current consumption.

**402 · quota exceeded**

```text
HTTP/1.1 402 Payment Required

{
  "error": {
    "code": "STORAGE_PROJECT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED",
    "message": "Project storage limit reached…",
    "details": { "quota": "storage_project_bytes", "limit": 1073741824, "used": 1073741824 }
  }
}
```

| Status | Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `402` | `STORAGE_PROJECT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | A legacy per-project storage cap is full (grandfathered plans) |
| `402` | `STORAGE_ACCOUNT_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | The organization’s shared storage capacity is full |
| `413` | `STORAGE_FILE_TOO_LARGE` | The file exceeds the plan or bucket maximum |
| `402` | `STORAGE_BANDWIDTH_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | The monthly total bandwidth budget (API + file delivery) is exhausted |
| `403` | `STORAGE_BUCKET_ACCESS_DENIED` | The caller cannot access this bucket |
| `410` | `STORAGE_UPLOAD_EXPIRED` | The upload session expired; start a new one |
| `404` | `STORAGE_OBJECT_NOT_FOUND` | No such object — or it is private and you cannot see it |
| `409` | `storage_object_exists` | The path is taken; pass `overwrite: true` to replace |
| `415` | `storage_mime_not_allowed` | The MIME type is not in the bucket allowlist |

Private objects never leak their existence: an unauthorized caller gets the same `404` as for a missing object.

## Additional resources

- [Platform quotas](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/quotas) Database and end-user limits alongside storage.
- [Pricing](https://cubibase.com/pricing) The published numbers per plan.

title: Storage security
text:
# Storage security

Source: https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/security

Also available: [Markdown version](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/security.md) · [llms.txt](https://cubibase.com/llms.txt) · [full site content](https://cubibase.com/llms-full.txt)

Storage reuses the platform’s identity and authorization model. Project isolation, path safety, and token scoping are enforced on the server, not delegated to the client.

## Project and tenant isolation

- The project is resolved from the request host and the API key — a client-supplied project id is never authoritative.
- Physical S3 keys are namespaced by project and bucket uuids; the catalog lives in each project’s own database.
- A key from one project presented to another project’s host is rejected.
- Secret API keys are privileged within their project only: they cannot cross projects, bypass quotas, or skip audit logging.

## Path and key safety

- Logical paths are validated: relative only, no `..` segments, no backslashes, no control characters, no empty or dot segments, no leading or trailing slash.
- Filenames never become S3 keys. The physical key is an opaque platform-generated identifier, so path tricks cannot reach another object.
- Upload policies pin one exact staging key and the exact declared size; a leaked policy cannot write anywhere else or store more bytes than were reserved.
- Staging objects are never publicly downloadable and are cleaned up on expiry.

## Tokens and credentials

- Signed download tokens are scoped to one object and one project, expire quickly, and are verified server-side; tampered or expired tokens fail with `401`.
- AWS credentials never reach clients. The S3 bucket blocks all public access, enforces TLS-only access and server-side encryption, and is reachable only through the engine’s least-privilege IAM role.
- Public buckets expose read-only object bytes — never listings of private metadata, never write paths.

> **important**: Treat secret API keys like database passwords: server-side only. For browser and mobile clients use the publishable key plus end-user JWTs, and signed links for sharing.

## Additional resources

- [API keys](https://cubibase.com/docs/platform/api-keys) Publishable versus secret keys.
- [Downloads and sharing](https://cubibase.com/docs/storage/downloads) Signed links in practice.
